en: *Chang Suozhi Lun* (Treatise on Manifesting What is Known), Volume One.
Composed by the Imperial Preceptor Phagpa of the Yuan Dynasty.
Proclaimed and bestowed upon Faxing, the General Superintendent of the Buddhist Teachings for the regions of Jianghuai, Fujian, and elsewhere.
Homage to the Vajra Master!

Homage to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, the omniscient ones who perceive all that is knowable and out of compassion reveal it to all beings! Homage to supreme wisdom! May you now expound upon that which is to be known.

That is to say: the world of the vessel and its sentient beings, the dharmas of the path and the dharmas of the fruit, together with all unconditioned dharmas; briefly summarized, these are enumerated as five.

Chapter One: The World of the Vessel. Regarding the essential substance that constitutes the world of the vessel, it is the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), because they possess the capacity for production.
Earth is solid, water is moist, fire is warm, and wind is mobile.
Among these great elements (*mahābhūta*), that which is most extremely subtle is called the "ultimate atom" (*paramāṇu*), also known as the "neighboring atom" (*aṇu*); it cannot be fully explained.
Seven of those atoms constitute one subtle atom (*paramāṇu*); seven of those subtle atoms constitute one mote of dust;
seven of those motes of dust constitute one particle that penetrates gold; seven of those particles that penetrate gold constitute one particle that penetrates water;
seven of those particles that penetrate water constitute one particle of a rabbit’s hair; and seven of those particles of a rabbit’s hair constitute one particle of a sheep’s hair.
Seven particles of sheep’s wool dust constitute one particle of cow’s hair dust; seven particles of cow’s hair dust constitute one particle of mote-dust in a sunbeam;
seven particles of mote-dust constitute one measure of nit; seven measures of nit constitute one measure of louse;
seven measures of louse constitute one measure of barley grain; and seven measures of barley grain constitute one finger-joint.
Three finger-joints constitute one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*); twenty-four finger-breadths laid side by side constitute one cubit (*hasta*);
four cubits constitute one bow (*dhanus*); five hundred bows constitute one *krośa*; and eight *krośas* constitute one *yojana*.
This is the measurement of the physical form of the world-system.
It is the cause for the formation of the world-system, brought about by the collective karma of all sentient beings.
How is it formed?
From within the realm of space, winds arise from the ten directions; striking one another yet remaining firm, dense, and unmoving, they form the wondrous wind-wheel (*vāyu-maṇḍala*).
It is azure-white in color, exceedingly vast and solid, sixteen *lakṣa* yojanas in depth, and immeasurable in its breadth.

From heat, clouds arise called the "Golden Treasury" (Kañcanagarbha), which pour down great rains; these rest upon the wind and are known as the "Bottom Ocean" (Tala-samudra), eleven lakṣas and twenty thousand yojanas in depth, and twelve lakṣas and three thousand four hundred and fifty yojanas in breadth.

As that water is struck by agitation, it solidifies above into gold, like the film that forms on the surface of boiled milk when it cools; this is the Golden Wheel (kāñcanamaṇḍala). Thus, the water wheel diminishes until its thickness is only eight lakṣas [yojanas].
The remainder transforms into gold, three hundred and twenty thousand yojanas in thickness.
The extent of the golden wheel is equal to that of the water wheel; its circumference is three times this, totaling three million six hundred and one thousand three hundred and fifty yojanas.
Below that wind-wheel at the base of the Sahā world-system are the earth and water wheels at the base of the four-continent world-system.
Upon the earth wheel, great rain falls again, which immediately forms the great ocean.

Struck and compressed by the wind, the superior grade of matter aggregates to form Mount Sumeru; the middling grade aggregates to form the seven golden mountains; the inferior grade aggregates to form the Cakravāḍa mountain range; and the miscellaneous grades aggregate to form the four continents and so forth.
The substance of that Mount Sumeru consists of silver in the east, lapis lazuli in the south, crystal in the west, and gold in the north;
the remaining seven mountains consist solely of gold;
and the lands of the four continents and other such features are composed of various materials.
That Cakravāḍa mountain is composed solely of iron.
As for the dimensions of Sumeru, it enters eighty thousand yojanas into the water; compared to all other mountains, it is preeminent and sublime, and is thus named "Wondrously High" (Sumeru).
Thereafter, the seven successive golden mountains are as follows: first, Mount Yugandhara, forty thousand yojanas in height;
second, Mount Īṣādhara, twenty thousand yojanas in height.
Third is Mount Khadiraka, ten thousand yojanas in height.
Fourth is Mount Sudarśana, five thousand yojanas in height.
Fifth is Mount Aśvakarṇa, two thousand five hundred yojanas in height.
The sixth is Mount Vinataka, twelve hundred and fifty *yojana*s in height.
The seventh is Mount Nimindhara, six hundred and twenty-five *yojana*s in height. The *Zanglun shu* (Commentary on the Abhidharmakośa) states: first, Yugandhara; second, Īṣādhara; third, Khadiraka;

fourth, Sudarśana; fifth, Aśvakarṇa; sixth, Vinitaka; seventh, Nimindhara. (Note: The text here lists "Vinitaka" as the sixth, whereas the standard sequence places it as the fifth; the commentary provides the standard list.)

Outside the four great continents is the Cakravāḍa mountain range, three hundred and twelve and a half yojanas high; their respective widths are each equal to the height of the water they emerge from.
The places where the various nāga kings sport among the seven golden mountains are called the Playful Seas (*krīḍā-samudra*).
Among the seven seas situated between the eight mountains near Mount Sumeru, the first is the Yugaṃdhara Sea, eighty thousand yojanas in breadth;
the second is the Īṣādhara Sea, forty thousand yojanas in breadth.
Third is the Khadira-ko Sea, twenty thousand yojanas in width;
fourth is the Sudarśana Sea, ten thousand yojanas in width;
fifth is the Aśvakarna Sea, five thousand yojanas in width.
The sixth sea, the Vinītaka, is two thousand five hundred yojanas wide;
the seventh sea, the Nimindhara, is one thousand two hundred and fifty yojanas wide, filled with water possessing the eight virtues.
The eight mountains and seven seas are all square in shape; the water of the outer sea is salty in taste.

From Mount Nimindhara to Mount Cakravāḍa, the distance between these two mountains is three hundred and twenty-two thousand yojanas. Although there is no actual division in the waters of the outer ocean, they are called the "four seas" because they manifest various colors according to the hue of Mount Sumeru: the eastern sea is white, the southern sea is blue, the western sea is red, and the northern sea is yellow.
Its circumference is thirty-six lakṣas and seven hundred and fifty yojanas;
the outer Cakravāḍa mountain range has a circumference of thirty-six lakṣas and two thousand six hundred and twenty-five yojanas.

Beyond that, the southern continent of Jambudvīpa is shaped like a carriage box; it is three yojanas and a half wide toward the Iron Ring Mountains (Cakravāḍa), while its other three sides are each two thousand yojanas, making its total circumference six thousand three yojanas and a half.
There are two intermediate continents: to the east is Cāmara, translated as "Cat-ox," and to the west is Varacāmara, translated as "Superior Cat-ox.
At the center of Jambudvīpa lies the kingdom of Magadha, the birthplace of all Buddhas of the three periods of time.

Next, proceeding north from here across nine Black Mountains, there is a great Snowy Mountain named Śrīghana (Possessing Auspiciousness). On the northern side of that mountain is Mount Gandhamādana (Fragrant Intoxication).
Between these two mountains dwells a great Nāga King named Anavatapta (Free from Heat); the lake where he resides is called Anavatapta, which in this language means "Free from Heat."
Its shape is square, with each side measuring fifty yojanas and a circumference of two hundred yojanas; the pool is filled everywhere with water of eight meritorious qualities.

From within this pool issue four great rivers: to the east is the Gaṅgā River, which flows from the mouth of an elephant with silver sands, and together with five hundred tributary streams, flows into the eastern sea;
to the south is the Sindhu River, which flows from the mouth of an ox with lapis lazuli sands, and together with five hundred tributary streams, flows into the southern sea.
The River Vaṅkṣu flows from the horse’s mouth with crystal sand, and together with five hundred tributary rivers, it flows into the western ocean;
the River Sītā flows from the lion’s mouth with golden sand, and together with five hundred tributary rivers, it flows into the northern ocean.
These four rivers flow from the Anavatapta Lake, circling it seven times to the right before proceeding in their respective directions.

Twenty yojanas to the north of Mount Gandhamādana lies a cliff named Nanda-śilā; each of its sides measures fifty yojanas, its circumference is two hundred yojanas, and its height is three and a half yojanas.

Furthermore, there were eight thousand small caves. Twenty yojanas to the north of these caves stood the king of śāla trees named Supratiṣṭhita; its roots extended forty bows into the earth, it was eighty bows in height, and it was surrounded by seven rows of trees arranged in succession.
Twenty yojanas to the east lies the Pond of Slow Currents; it is circular in shape, fifty yojanas in width, and one hundred and fifty yojanas in circumference.

Furthermore, there are eight thousand small ponds filled with water possessing the eight virtues; within them grow lotuses whose leaves are like ox-hide, whose stalks are like axles, whose flowers are like chariot wheels, and whose flavor is as sweet as honey.

In this place there is also the elephant king named Supratiṣṭhita, whom Śakra mounts when approaching battle; accompanied by eight thousand elephants, he dwells at the Golden Rock during the four months of winter, at the Abode of Good Dwelling during the four months of summer, and at the Pool of Slow Flowing Streams during the four months of the rainy season.
Beside the Lake Anavatapta stands a Jambū tree; its fruits are delicious and as large as jars. When they ripen and fall into the water, they produce the sound "jambū.
Dragons transform into fish and swallow these fruits; the remnants that encounter the current turn into Jambū gold. Because of the name of this tree, it is called Jambudvīpa.
To the west of this continent lies the country of Oḍḍiyāna, where the Great Vajra Palace is situated and the lineage-holders reside; from there, the Vajrayāna teachings were transmitted.
In the midst of the Southern Sea is a mountain called Potalaka, where the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara dwells upon its summit, and the Noble Mother Tārā resides at its base.

To the east are five peaks where Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva resides; there are sixteen great kingdoms and a thousand minor kingdoms, as well as three hundred and sixty kinds of people and seven hundred and twenty varieties of distinct languages.

To the east of that outer sea is the continent called Pūrvavideha; it is shaped like a half-moon, measuring three hundred and fifty yojanas along the side facing Mount Sumeru, sixty yojanas along the other sides, and six thousand three hundred and fifty yojanas in circumference.
On the two sides of that continent are two intermediate continents: Uttarakuru (translated as "Body" in Chinese) to the north, and Aparagoyānī (translated as "Superior Body" in Chinese) to the south.

These three continents surpass the other continents by the height of seven *tāla* trees; alternatively, it is said that because the people of these continents possess dignified and handsome features, and their bodies are superior, they are called "Superior Body."
Beyond that outer sea is the northern continent called Kuru; its shape is square with four equal sides, each measuring two thousand yojanas, for a total circumference of eight thousand yojanas.

On the two sides of that continent are two intermediate continents: the first is named Kuru, which means "Possessing Excellence," and the second is Gaurasa, which means "Possessing the Side of Excellence.

All the enjoyments of the people on those continents issue from wish-fulfilling trees (*kalpavṛkṣa*). Seven days before their death, these wish-fulfilling trees produce an unpleasant sound, announcing: "In seven days you shall die."
Some say that the people of this continent have lowly tongues and speak with the voices of flesh-eating demons; therefore, it is called Kuru, which means "unpleasant sound.

To the west of the outer ocean lies the continent called Godānīya, shaped like a full moon, measuring two thousand five hundred yojanas in diameter and seven thousand five hundred yojanas in circumference.
There are two intermediate continents: to the south is Śāṭhā (translated here as "Possessing Deceit"), and to the north is Uttaramantriṇa (translated here as "Superior Manner").
Because the people of those continents possess many precious cattle for trade, they are called the Continent of Go-dānīya (Cattle-Trade).
The oceans, mountains, and so forth extend downward for eighty thousand yojanas, because they are adjacent to the Golden Ground (*kāñcanamayī bhūmiḥ*).
Those [oceans] adjacent to Jambudvīpa, Śālmala-dvīpa, Suvarṇa-dvīpa, Candra-dvīpa, and so on, belong to Jambudvīpa.
The other great continents and their minor sub-continents are likewise.

Forty thousand yojanas above the sky, in a realm that is pure and unobstructed, there is a supreme, solid wind-circle (vāyu-maṇḍala) that rotates from right to left; upon it, the sun, moon, stars, and the celestial beings dwelling in the air rely for their abode.
The solar disk is composed of fire-crystal; it is fifty-one yojanas in diameter, one hundred and fifty-three yojanas in circumference, and six yojanas and eighteen parts in thickness.
Above, there is a golden rim, upon which gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, and white jade form four corners in relief.
The palaces where the Sun Deity and others reside are set in motion by the winds, circling the four great continents once every day and night.
When the sun moves northward, the days become long; when it moves southward, they are short; and when it moves between the two, day and night are equal.
Due to its movement through these regions, light produces cold and heat, which constitute the transitions between winter and summer.
Traveling north for six months and south for six months, when they reach the middle path, it is called the "revolving wheel of the sun and moon. The completion of this circuit is termed one year.

As for the lunar disk, it is composed of water-crystal; it is fifty *yojanas* in diameter and one hundred and fifty *yojanas* in circumference. It is six *yojanas* and eighteen fractional parts thick, and upon its surface there are further exquisite formations of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal, arranged in four corners.

Regarding the palaces inhabited by the Moon Deity and others, the waxing and waning of their own shadows—caused by the varying distance between the sun and moon—is as follows: through the increase of one part, the first half-month arises; when fifteen parts are complete, it is called "full"; and through the decrease of one part, the second half-month arises.

When its own shadow has finished covering fifteen parts of it, it is said to be "not full. Because of this increase and decrease, it is called "the empty mansion" (*nakṣatra*); because of one day and night, it is called "the mansion-ground" (*nakṣatrabhūmi*).
Thirty such days constitute one month.

As for the constellations, the celestial palaces of the Ākāśavāsin deities are composed of various jewels; they are all circular in shape—the small ones being one *go-vyūha* [the distance of a cow's bellow], the medium ones three *go-vyūhas*, and the large ones six *go-vyūhas*—and their circumference is three times that size, where the hosts of the Four Great Kings reside.
Mount Sumeru has four terraces. Starting from the water's edge and extending upward for ten thousand yojanas is the first terrace;
extending sixteen thousand yojanas outward from the side of Mount Sumeru and rising upward for ten thousand yojanas is the second terrace;
extending eight thousand yojanas outward and rising upward for ten thousand yojanas is the third terrace.
It extends four thousand yojanas outward and rises ten thousand yojanas upward, forming four tiers.

It extends two thousand yojanas outward; at the summit of that Mount Sumeru, there are four peaks, one at each corner, four and a half yojanas high, one hundred and twenty-five yojanas wide, and five hundred yojanas in circumference, where yakṣa deities dwell.

At the center of the Heaven of the Thirty-three atop this mountain peak is a city called Sudarśana, composed entirely of pure gold; it is one and a half yojanas high, each side is two thousand five hundred yojanas, and its circumference is ten thousand yojanas.
The body of that city is made of gold and is adorned with one hundred and one varieties of miscellaneous jewels.
Its ground is as soft as *tūla* cotton.
On the four sides of this city, there are sixteen thousand jeweled pillars, jeweled beams, jeweled rafters, and jeweled eaves.
It has four sides and four gates; furthermore, there are thousands of minor gates within the main ones, and from the four great thoroughfares branch out various smaller lanes.
Beside each of the four gates stand five hundred devaputras, all clad in sturdy armor, guarding these gates.

Within the city is the palace of Śakra, called the Supreme Abode (Vaijayanta) and also the Palace of Excellence; it is square in shape, four hundred and fifty yojanas in height, with each side measuring two hundred and fifty yojanas, and a circumference of one thousand yojanas.

There are one hundred and one defensive towers; each defensive tower has seven pavilions, each precious pavilion has seven small pavilions, each small pavilion has seven ponds, and each pond has seven lotuses. Upon each lotus are seven boys and seven girls, performing various kinds of music and enjoying themselves with song and dance.
To the east of the city of Sudarśana is the Grove of Various Vehicles (Citraratha), one thousand yojanas in height;

to the south, bordering the battlefield, is the Grove of Coarseness (Raudra); to the west, the place of various activities, is the Grove of Intermixture (Saṃbhinna); and to the north, the place of recreation, is the Grove of Joy (Nandana). Their length and breadth are the same as those previously mentioned.

Beyond these gardens and others by twenty yojanas lies the "Good Ground" known as Saṃjīva (Reviving), Pāruṣyaka (Coarse), Aśoka (Sorrowless), and Caitraratha (Chariot of the Gods); their dimensions are equal to those of the four gardens.

To the northeast of Sudarśana stands the wish-fulfilling tree named Pārijāta, also called the Maṇḍāravatī; its roots extend fifty yojanas deep, it rises one hundred yojanas high, and its branches spread fifty yojanas wide, capable of bestowing all desired pleasures.
Below is a flat rock called Arimālīka, white in color like fine cotton cloth, fifty yojanas on each side and two hundred yojanas in circumference.
To the southwest of Sudarśana is the assembly hall of the devas, named Sudharmā, which is nine hundred yojanas in circumference and circular in shape.

In the center of this hall is the throne of Śakra, made entirely of pure gold; surrounding this throne are the seats of thirty-two ministers, all of whom are stationed throughout the Heaven of the Thirty-three.

Ascending eighty thousand yojanas into the realm of space, it rests upon the wind; this celestial palace of the Yāma devas, composed of various jewels, is twice the size of the summit of Mount Sumeru.

Ascending sixteen million yojanas, it rests upon the wind within the realm of space; the Tuṣita celestial palace, composed of various jewels, is equal in measure to the Suyāma heaven, being twice as long and wide.

Ascending three hundred and twenty thousand yojanas, it rests upon the wind within the realm of space; the celestial palaces of the Nirmāṇarati devas, composed of various jewels, are equal in size to those of Tuṣita, being twice as long and wide.

Ascending sixty-four hundred thousand *yojanas* into the midst of space, it rests upon the wind; there lies the palace of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin devas, composed of various jewels, equal in size to that of the Nirmāṇarati heaven, yet twice as vast in length and breadth.
This is the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

Above it is the first dhyāna. Thus, the four continents, the seven mountain ranges, Mount Sumeru, the Cakravāḍa mountains, the six heavens of the desire realm, and the first dhyāna together constitute what is called a "four-continent world-system" (*cāturdvīpaka-lokadhātu*). A thousand of these constitutes a "small thousandfold world-system" (*sāhasra-cūḍika-lokadhātu*), which is encircled by a single Iron Ring Mountain (*Cakravāḍa*).
When one thousand of these small chiliocosms are counted together, they constitute a medium chiliocosm, which is surrounded by a single Iron Ring Mountain (*Cakravāḍa*).
When one thousand of these medium chiliocosms are counted together, they constitute a trichiliocosm, which is surrounded by a single Great Iron Ring Mountain.
In this manner, there are ten billion such world-systems of four continents, all distributed throughout space.
In the dark regions between the Iron Ring Mountains (*Cakravāḍa*) and other mountains and continents, there is neither day nor night; one cannot see even a hand raised before one's face.

The extent of the Heaven of the First Dhyāna is equal to the four continents; the extent of the Heaven of the Second Dhyāna is equal to a small chiliocosm; the extent of the Heaven of the Third Dhyāna is equal to a medium chiliocosm; and the extent of the Heaven of the Fourth Dhyāna is equal to a trichiliocosm. The distances between them all increase twofold respectively; this is called the Form Realm (Rūpadhātu).

As for the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there is no distinct location; if there are those born there, they pass away in whatever place they were and are reborn in that very same place. Because they abide in the formless meditative absorptions (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), it is called "formless."

Chapter Two: The World of Sentient Beings. Regarding the world of sentient beings, there are in total six types: first, hell-beings; second, hungry ghosts; third, animals; fourth, humans; fifth, non-gods (asuras); and sixth, gods.
What are the meanings of these six names? They are as follows:

because their limbs are hacked and mangled, they are called hell-beings (*naraka*); because they are oppressed by hunger and thirst, they are called hungry ghosts (*preta*); because they move while lying on their sides, they are called animals (*tiryagyoni*); and because their minds involve much conceptual discrimination, they are called humans (*manuṣya*).

Regarding the meaning of *asura*: although their bodies and enjoyments are similar to those of the gods (*deva*), they are slightly inferior; alternatively, because they lack wine (*sura*), they are called "non-gods.

Regarding the meaning of *asura* [as a term for a class of beings]: they are born from the body of Brahmā, engage in play and entertainment, or are worthy of offerings; thus they are called "gods," which is the meaning of *deva*.

As for the hells, they lie twenty thousand yojanas beneath Jambudvīpa; they extend twenty thousand yojanas across in all four directions and are composed entirely of iron, with flames blazing intensely.

There are eight hot hells: first, Sañjīva (Reviving); second, Kālasūtra (Black Rope); third, Saṃghāta (Crushing); fourth, Raurava (Howling); fifth, Mahāraurava (Great Howling); sixth, Tapana (Heating); seventh, Pratāpana (Great Heating); and eighth, Avīci (Uninterrupted).

As for the Reviving Hell (*saṃjīva*), sentient beings born there, impelled by their past karma, seize various weapons and give rise to mutual resentment and hatred, hacking and harming one another until they fall limb from limb, fainting and dying momentarily.
When the sound of emptiness resonates once more, those sentient beings are restored to life and again slaughter one another.
As for their lifespan, one lifetime of the gods of the Four Great Kings constitutes a single day and night; calculated in this manner, they endure such suffering for five hundred years.
As for the Black Rope Hell, its wardens and attendants mark the bodies of sentient beings from head to foot with black lines, then dismember their limbs using flaming saws and battle-axes.
Due to the power of their prior karma, they are released from below and reborn above.
As for their lifespan, one lifetime in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven constitutes a single day and night; calculated in this manner, they endure such suffering for a thousand years.

As for the Saṃghāta Hell, when sentient beings are born there, they are struck with iron hammers; alternatively, two iron mountains shaped like ram's heads come together, grinding and crushing them. When the two mountains open, they are restored to life naturally, only to be crushed and destroyed once again.

Regarding their lifespan: one lifetime of the gods who dwell free from strife constitutes a single day and night; calculated in this manner, they endure such torment for a lifespan of two thousand years.
As for the Hell of Wailing: sentient beings born there enter a dense forest within a terrifying, heated iron pool, where blazing flames burn them perpetually for ages.
By the power of their prior karma, their tongues become a thousand yojanas in length and breadth.
There is a great ox with iron horns and iron armor; yoked to an iron plowshare, its tongue is furrowed by the plow as flames blaze intensely.
As for its lifespan, one lifetime in the Tuṣita Heaven constitutes a single day and night; calculated in this manner, it undergoes such suffering for four thousand years.
As for the Hell of Great Screaming, it is the same as the preceding one, but its suffering is doubled.

Regarding its lifespan: the duration of one lifetime in the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations constitutes a single day and night; calculated in this manner, they endure such torment for eight thousand years.
As for the Hell of Intense Heat (Pratāpana), it consists of three layers of iron walls through which flames penetrate; therein one suffers agonizing pain.

Regarding its lifespan: the duration of a single lifetime in the Heaven of Controlling Others' Emanations (Paranirmita-vaśavartin) constitutes one day and night there; with such a reckoning, one undergoes this suffering for sixteen thousand years.
As for the Hell of Intense Heat (*Pratāpana*), it is likewise like the preceding one, but its suffering is doubled.
As for its lifespan, it lasts for half an intermediate kalpa (*antarakalpa*), during which one undergoes such torments.
As for the Avīci Hell, within an iron chamber, one’s body becomes a single mass of flames and undergoes extreme torment.
Its lifespan is equal to one intermediate kalpa (*antarakalpa*).
As for the sixteen *utsada* hells, there are four locations on each side adjacent to the eight hot hells.

First is the *Kukūla* (Heated Embers) hell; it is knee-deep, and when sentient beings wander there, as soon as they set foot down, their skin, flesh, and blood are all scorched and sloughed away, leaving only the bones behind.
When they lift their feet, the flesh grows back again, restored exactly as it was before.

Second is the Excrement Mire (*gūthakardama*), an impure mire of filth where sentient beings sink up to their waists; therein dwell many *kṛmuka* worms with mouths as sharp as needles, which bore through the skin and penetrate the bone to devour the marrow.
The third is the Razor-Blade Increase (*asipattravana*), which further comprises three types:

First, the Path of Razor Blades (*asipattramārga*). This refers to a great road strewn with razor blades laid face-up; when sentient beings wander there, as soon as they set foot upon it, their skin, flesh, and blood are all sliced and shattered and fall away.

When they lift their feet, the parts regenerate and return to their original state. Second, the Forest of Sword-Leaves (*asi-patra-vana*). This refers to a forest where the trees have exclusively sharp, keen swords for leaves. When sentient beings wander there, the wind blows the leaves down, hacking and piercing their limbs so that their flesh and bones fall apart. There are spotted crows and dogs that tear and devour them.

The third forest of iron thorns is named *Tīkṣṇa-māli*. This means that the trees of this forest have sharp iron thorns sixteen finger-widths long. When sentient beings are driven to climb up and down these trees, those thorns—extremely sharp—pierce them upward and downward. The flesh, blood, and skin of these beings hang and stick to the thorns until only their sinews and bones remain.
There are iron-beaked crows that peck out the eyes and brain-marrow of sentient beings, competing with one another to devour them.

Although the three types of paths, such as the Path of Sword-Blades, differ from one another, they share the same iron weapons; therefore, they are subsumed within a single *ūrdhva-gamana* (increasing) hell.

The fourth *Uṣṇa-niraya* (Hell of Boiling Water) is named *Ataraṇīya* (Unfordable). It is filled everywhere with extremely hot caustic alkaline water. When sentient beings enter it, they either float or sink, move against the current or with it, or drift sideways or upright; they are steamed and boiled until their flesh and bones are reduced to pulp. It is like a great cauldron filled with caustic liquid, placed over a fierce fire beneath which rice and the like are set; as the rice turns and rolls up and down within it, its entire body becomes a mass of mush, and so it is for the sentient beings there.
Should they wish to escape, there are various hell-wardens on both banks who, grasping swords and spears, block their way and force them back; there is no means by which they can emerge.
This river is like a moat, while the three preceding ones are like gardens.
These are called the Neighboring Hells (*utsada-naraka*). As for the eight Cold Hells, they are:

first, Arbuda (Blister); second, Nirarbuda (Cracked Blister); third, Aṭaṭa; fourth, Hahava; fifth, Huhuva; sixth, Utpala (cracked like a blue lotus flower); seventh, Padma (cracked like a lotus flower); and eighth, Mahāpadma (cracked like a great lotus flower).
As for the Arbuda Hell (the Blistering Hell), beings are born amidst cold waters; because of extreme and severe cold, blisters form upon their bodies, hence it is called the Arbuda Hell.

Regarding its lifespan: if one were to take eighty *dronas* of sesame seeds from the Magadha country and remove a single seed every hundred years, when those sesame seeds are exhausted, the lifespan there would likewise be spent.
In the Arbuda (Blister) Hell, due to extreme cold, their blisters burst and yellow fluid leaks out.
Their lifespan is double that of the previous [hell], being twenty [intermediate kalpas].
In the Atata Hell, due to intense cold, they endure by gnashing their teeth.
As for their lifespan, it is twice that of the preceding twenty [kalpas].
As for the Ababa Hell, its inhabitants utter sounds of endurance against the cold.
Their lifespan is twice that of the preceding twenty [kalpas].
In the *Utkūla-niraya* (the Hell of Choking Sobs), one utters these sounds of suffering by weeping from the cold.
As for its lifespan, it is double that of the previous twenty [kalpas].
In the *Utpala-puṣpa-vibhinna-niraya* (the Hell of Being Split Like an Utpala Flower), the body is split by the intense cold, like the petals of an *utpala* flower.
As for their lifespan, it is double that of the former twenty [kalpas].
As for those in the Lotus-Splitting Hell, their bodies split apart due to the intense cold like a blooming lotus flower.
Their lifespan is double that of the former twenty [kalpas].
As for those in the Hell of Splitting Like a Great Lotus, their bodies split apart even more than before, like a great lotus flower in full bloom with many petals.
Their lifespan is double that of the previous twenty [kalpas].
The solitary hells are located in the wilderness mountains of Jambudvīpa; because there, one experiences a mixture of suffering and pleasure for the duration of a single day and night.
The eight hot hells, the eight cold hells, the neighboring hells, and the solitary hells—these are collectively known as the eighteen hells.
As for the hungry ghosts (preta): five hundred yojanas below the city of Rājagṛha, there is a city of hungry ghosts named Yellow-White, also called Pale and Dismal.
Its king is the Dharma King Yama, who dwells together with thirty-six classes of retinues.

There are four such categories: first, external obstacles; second, internal obstacles; third, obstacles regarding food and drink; and fourth, obstacles to food and drink. Regarding the first, external obstacles:
one is unable to hear even the sounds of food and drink.
Second, as for internal obstacles: even if one obtains a small amount of food and drink, it cannot enter because the mouth is like the eye of a needle;
even if it can enter the mouth, it cannot pass through because the throat is like a horse's tail-hair;
even if it passes the throat, the belly is like a mountain cavern and cannot be filled.
Although their bellies are full, their shanks are like blades of grass, unable to move; they undergo this great suffering.
Third, regarding the obstacle of food and drink: when they see food and drink, immeasurable hell-wardens brandishing various weapons guard it so that they cannot obtain any.

Regarding those with four obstacles to food and drink: when they eat and drink, due to the retribution of their karma, iron balls and molten copper are poured into their mouths and flow out from below.
These four types are all hungry ghosts.

Regarding their lifespan: one month among humans constitutes a single day and night; calculated in this manner, their life span is five hundred years, which corresponds to fifteen thousand years among humans.
Those who dwell in places such as the human world or cold forests, and subsist on flesh and blood, all belong to the class of hungry ghosts (*preta*).

Third, as for animals (*tiryagyoni*), they mostly dwell in rivers and oceans, living in dense swarms like dregs of wine; the large devour the small, and the small devour the large, as they live in mutual terror.
Because they dwell amidst the waves and billows of the ocean, their abodes are not fixed; they may reside among humans or devas.
As for their lifespan, it is as long as that of a nāga king, lasting half an intermediate kalpa (antarakalpa), or as short as that of a gnat and the like, lasting but a single kṣaṇa.
The dimensions of their bodies are not fixed.
Fourth, as for "humans," they dwell on the four great continents, the eight intermediate continents, and various smaller islands.

Regarding their lifespan: for the people of Jambudvīpa, at the time of the initial formation of the kalpa, their lifespan was immeasurable; thereafter it gradually decreased until it reached sixty years, and subsequently it gradually decreased further down to ten years, after which it increases again, with no fixed measure.

The inhabitants of Uttarakuru have a fixed lifespan of one thousand years; those of Pūrvavideha have a lifespan of five hundred years; and those of Aparagoyānī have a lifespan of two hundred and fifty years.
With the exception of those in Uttarakuru, the others are subject to untimely death and calamities.
As for their enjoyments: in the northern continent of Kuru, they eat natural rice, and their clothing and ornaments emerge from wish-fulfilling trees;
those in the other three continents eat grains, meat, and so forth, and possess wealth and resources for their enjoyment.
As for their physical stature: the people of Jambudvīpa measure eight cubits; those of Aparagoyānī measure sixteen cubits; and those of Uttarakuru measure thirty-two cubits.
The facial features of the people there are also shaped like the continents.
The people of the smaller sub-continents are also like those of the great continents, though their bodies are each reduced by half; therefore, it is described in this way.

Fifth, as for the non-gods (asuras): ten thousand one hundred yojanas below the water’s edge of Mount Sumeru, within the city of Radiance amidst the vast expanse of the mountain, resides the Asura King named Rāhu (translated here as "Seizer of the Brain"), together with his retinue.
Furthermore, beyond eleven thousand yojanas, within the city of Tārāmālā, resides the asura king named Gṛhamaṇi with his retinue.
Again, beyond eleven thousand yojanas, within the city of Dṛḍhā, resides the asura king named Sumukha, also called Mahābala, with his retinue.

Furthermore, ten thousand one hundred yojanas beyond, within the city of Gambhīra, dwells the asura king named Vemacitra—translated as "Various Silks" or "Tattooed Body"—who resides with his many retinues and constantly engages in rivalry and combat with Śakra.

The city is called Suvarṇavatī; the palace is named Saṃgītita; the king of wish-fulfilling trees is named Tāmbūlika; the place of assembly is named Bhadraśrī; the stone is named Subhadra; the gardens are named Samantaprīti, Suprīti, Varaprīti, and Atiprītisubha; the grounds are likewise named Samantaprīti, Suprīti, Varaprīti, and Atiprīti; the elephant ridden when approaching battle is named Aparājita; the elephant ridden for recreation is named Himavanta; and the horse is named Tuṅganāsa.
These Asuras contended with the Thirty-three Gods for the *sudhā* nectar and the Apsaras maidens.

For the sake of this battle, they emerged from the mountain fastnesses, clad in sturdy armor of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, and *sphaṭika*; holding swords, spears, javelins, bows, and arrows in their hands, they led their fourfold armies.
Those Asura kings—Rāhu, Kharaskandha, Mucilinda, Vemacitrin, and others—either came in groups of three or all four together.

At that time, Śakra’s five protective hosts—the first being the assembly led by the Dragon King Playful Ocean-Vow-Delight-in-White-Dharma—engaged in battle with the asura armies and caused them to turn back.
If the dragon was not victorious, he went to where Sthiraśiras was; together with those two as his protectors, he again engaged in battle with the asuras.
If he was not victorious there either, he went to where Mālyadhara was; together with those three as his protectors, he again engaged in battle.
Furthermore, if he does not prevail, he goes to the abode of the Ever-Arrogant (Nityoddhata), where he fights again with four guardians.
If he still does not prevail, he goes to the abode of the Four Great Kings (Cāturmahārāja), where he fights again with five guardians.
The Four Great Heavenly Kings led their fourfold armies, clad in precious, sturdy armor and wielding various spears and weapons; in most battles, the Four Heavenly Kings were victorious.
If they were unable to repel them, they would go before the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and say to Śakra:
"We have guarded [this realm] but cannot turn back those hosts of asuras; Your Majesty should yourself repel the enemy."
Having made this announcement, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, mounted the elephant Airāvaṇa and addressed the assembly of the Trāyastriṃśa gods, saying:
"You should know that the army of the asuras has now reached the summit of Mount Sumeru; you must don sturdy armor, take up your chariots, and go forth to battle the asuras."

Having spoken these words, those devaputras each donned precious armor and grasped spears and weapons; they departed from the Garden of Many Chariots to take their respective vehicles, entered the Garden of Coarse Evil to further corrupt their bodies and minds, and emerged from the City of Good Vision to engage in mutual combat and battle with those asuras.
If the asuras prevail, they invade the city;
if the devas prevail, they pursue the asura army as far as the First Sea.
During the battle, when the devas and asuras sever their thighs or waists, they die instantly.
If their hands or feet were severed, they would grow back as they were before.

When the Bhagavān, a Pratyekabuddha, or a Cakravartin King dwells in the world, the Asuras do not give rise to contentious thoughts; even if they should engage in conflict, the devas will surely be victorious.
When wholesome qualities increase in the world, the devas prevail; when unwholesome qualities increase, the asuras prevail. Therefore, the devas protect and uphold virtuous deeds.
As for the devas, there are six in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), seventeen in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and four in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Regarding the six heavens of the desire realm: on the first tier of Mount Sumeru dwell the Karoṭapāṇis; on the second tier dwell the Mālādharas; and on the third tier dwell the Sadāmattas.
On the northern side of Mount Yugandhara, there is a city named Anaghāvatī, where the yakṣa hosts of the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa reside.
Likewise, in the east, there is a city named Bhadrāśva, where the Great Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra resides, and where the gandharva hosts dwell.
In the western direction there is a city named Citra; there dwells the Great Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa, and the host of nāgas resides there.
In the southern direction there is a city named Vardhana; there dwells the Great Heavenly King Virūḍhaka, and the host of kumbhāṇḍas resides there.

On the remaining four tiers, the seven golden mountains and so forth, as well as the sun, moon, and stars, the Cakravāḍa mountain range, the mountains of Jambudvīpa, and the Tāla trees—where the hosts of the Four Great Kings also dwell and reside—all of these belong to the Four Great Kings; this is called one division.
Regarding their lifespan: fifty human years constitute one day and night; thus, their lifespan extends for five hundred such years.
As for their physical stature, it is one-quarter of a krośa.

Upon the summit of Mount Sumeru, in the Heaven of the Thirty-three, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, dwells in his most excellent abode; together with the asura maiden named Subhā and a host of celestial maidens, he enjoys all manner of sensual pleasures without ever reaching satiety.

Furthermore, there was an elephant king named Sunābha whom he rode when facing battle; in the pleasure grove, there was an elephant king named Airāvata (translated here as "Son of the Earth-Sustainer"). Each of these two elephants had a circumference of seven yojanas, and each was attended by a retinue of eight thousand young elephants.
Furthermore, there is a horse-king named Swift Wind who dwells with eight thousand horses.
The ministers of the Lord of Heaven number thirty-three; for this reason, they are called the Heaven of the Thirty-three (Trāyastriṃśa).
When the sons of the gods are addicted to the pleasures of the five desires and become negligent, there appears a great celestial drum; from its sound issues a voice that warns the gods, saying:
"All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; all that is tainted is suffering; all dharmas are without self; nirvana is bliss."
When engaging in battle with the armies of the asuras, he utters sounds that eliminate suffering and issues this warning:
"May the devas be victorious; may the asuras be defeated.
Regarding the palaces, city walls, trees, and gathered stones, they are as previously explained.
Regarding the lifespan of those devas: one hundred human years constitute a single day and night; calculated in this manner, their lifespan is one thousand years.
As for the physical stature of those devas, it is half a yojana.
As for the Yāma devas, they are so named because they have departed from the disputes that the Trāyastriṃśa devas and asuras engage in.
Regarding the lifespan of those devas: two hundred human years constitute one day and night; by such calculation, their lifespan is two thousand years.
The stature of the gods there is two yojanas.

As for the Tuṣita Heaven, it is so called because the Honored One Maitreya, who succeeds to the position of the Dharma King of both mundane and supramundane dharmas, experiences great dharma-joy; "Tuṣita" thus carries the meaning of "all joy."
Four hundred human years constitute one day and night for that heaven; its lifespan is four thousand years, and the height of its inhabitants is four yojanas.
As for the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations (Nirmāṇarati), they are called "Delighting in Emanations" because they create their own objects of enjoyment.
Eight hundred years among humans constitute one day and night in that heaven; their lifespan is eight thousand years, and their physical stature is eight yojanas.
As for the Paranirmita-vaśavartin devas, they enjoy objects created by others, and thus they are called Paranirmita-vaśavartin (Masters over Others' Creations).
The king of that heaven possesses majestic power and sovereignty; he is the Lord of Māra.
One thousand six hundred human years constitute one day and night for that deva; his lifespan is sixteen thousand years, and his body measures sixteen yojanas in height.
From the Avīci Hell below up to the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven above, this is called the Desire Realm (kāmadhātu).
It is so designated because its inhabitants are addicted to sensual pleasures and subsist on edible food (kavaḍīkārāhāra).
Regarding the seventeen heavens of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), they are subsumed within the four dhyānas.
The three heavens of the first dhyāna are the Brahmakāyika, the Brahmapurohita, and the Mahābrahmā.
As for the lifespan in those heavens: it is half an eon (*kalpa*) for the Brahmakāyikas, one eon for the Brahmapurohitas, and one and a half eons for the Mahābrahmās.
The physical dimensions of those devas are, in successive order, half a yojana, one yojana, and one and a half yojanas.
As for the three heavens of the second dhyāna, they are called Parīttābha (Limited Light), Apramāṇābha (Immeasurable Light), and Ābhāsvara (Utmost Light).

Regarding the lifespans of those devas: for the Heaven of Limited Light (Parīttābhā), it is two kalpas; for the four heavens above that, forty intermediate kalpas constitute one great kalpa; for the heavens below that, eighty intermediate kalpas constitute one great kalpa; for the Heaven of Immeasurable Light (Apramāṇābhā), it is four kalpas; and for the Heaven of Ultimate Light (Ābhāsvarā), it is eight kalpas.
As for the body size of those devas: in the Heaven of Limited Light it is two yojanas; in the Heaven of Immeasurable Light, four yojanas; and in the Heaven of Ultimate Light, eight yojanas.
Regarding the three heavens of the third dhyāna, they are: Limited Virtue, Immeasurable Virtue, and Vast Virtue.
The lifespan of those devas is sixteen kalpas for those of minor merit, thirty-two kalpas for those of immeasurable merit, and sixty-four kalpas for those of extensive merit.
The body size of those devas is sixteen yojanas for those of minor merit, thirty-two yojanas for those of immeasurable merit, and sixty-four yojanas for those of extensive merit.
Regarding the eight heavens of the fourth dhyāna: Anabhraka (Cloudless), Puṇyaprasava (Merit-born), and Bṛhatphala (Vast Fruit)—these three are abodes for ordinary beings;

Anamāya (Without Affliction), Atapa (Without Heat), Sudṛśa (Good Appearance), Sudarśana (Good Vision), and Akaniṣṭha (Ultimate Form)—these five are abodes for noble ones, known as the Five Pure Abodes.

The lifespans of those devas are as follows: one hundred and twenty-five kalpas for the Anabhraka (Cloudless) devas; two hundred and fifty kalpas for the Puṇyaprasava (Merit-born) devas; five hundred kalpas for the Bṛhatphala (Vast Fruit) devas; one thousand kalpas for the Avṛha (Unafflicted) devas; two thousand kalpas for the Atapa (Heatless) devas; four thousand kalpas for the Sudṛśa (Good Appearance) devas; eight thousand kalpas for the Sudarśana (Good Vision) devas; and sixteen thousand kalpas for the Akaniṣṭha (Ultimate Form) devas.

The dimensions of those celestial bodies are as follows: one hundred and twenty-five yojanas for the Anabhraka (Cloudless) heaven, two hundred and fifty yojanas for the Puṇyaprasava (Merit-born) heaven, five hundred yojanas for the Bṛhatphala (Vast Fruit) heaven, one thousand yojanas for the Avṛha (Untroubled) heaven, two thousand yojanas for the Atapa (Heatless) heaven, four thousand yojanas for the Sudṛśa (Beautiful to Behold) heaven, eight thousand yojanas for the Sudarśana (Good to See) heaven, and sixteen thousand yojanas for the Akaniṣṭha (Ultimate Form) heaven.
From the Brahmakāyika heaven up to the Akaniṣṭha heaven, all are collectively termed the Form Realm (rūpadhātu).
Because they have transcended the pleasures of desire yet are not free from form, it is called the Form Realm.

As for the four heavens of the Formless Realm (ārūpyadhātu), they possess neither physical form nor spatial location; they are divided into four according to their meditative attainments: the Sphere of Infinite Space, the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness, the Sphere of Nothingness, and the Sphere of Neither Perception nor Non-perception.

Regarding the lifespans of those devas: in the Sphere of Infinite Space, the lifespan is twenty thousand great kalpas; in the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness, forty thousand great kalpas; in the Sphere of Nothingness, sixty thousand great kalpas; and in the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-Perception, eighty thousand great kalpas.

Those four locations refer to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*); because they are not free from the form of meditative concentration (*samādhi-rūpa*) and have emerged from coarse form (*audārika-rūpa*), they lack name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
Their lifespans are measured in years, eons (*kalpa*), and periods of time.

What is their measure? The shortest duration of time is called a *kṣaṇa*. One hundred and twenty *kṣaṇas* constitute one *tatkṣaṇa*. Sixty *tatkṣaṇas* constitute one *lava*. Thirty *lavas* constitute one *muhūrta*—which is translated here as "a brief interval" (*xūyú*). Thirty *muhūrtas* constitute one day and night. Thirty days and nights constitute one month. Twelve months constitute one year.

There are six kinds of kalpas: first, the intermediate kalpa (antarakalpa), also called the minor kalpa; second, the kalpa of formation (vivartakalpa); third, the kalpa of abiding (vivartasthāyikalpa); fourth, the kalpa of destruction (saṃvartakalpa); fifth, the kalpa of emptiness (saṃvartasthāyikalpa); and sixth, the great kalpa (mahākalpa).

Regarding one intermediate kalpa (*antarakalpa*): when the lifespan of the people of Jambudvīpa gradually decreases from an immeasurable number of years down to eighty thousand years, it is subsumed within the kalpa of formation (*vivartakalpa*).
From eighty thousand years, decreasing down to ten years, is called the beginning of an intermediate kalpa.
Increasing again by eighty thousand years until it decreases back to ten years constitutes one cycle of increase and decrease.
Eighteen such cycles of increase and decrease constitute eighteen intermediate kalpas (*antarakalpa*).

Thereafter, the lifespan increases from ten years up to eighty thousand years; this constitutes eighteen cycles of the middle period, which together with the preceding and succeeding periods make twenty middle kalpas.

Regarding the two kalpas of formation: beginning from the wind-circle up to the Avīci Hell, the formation of the vessel-world and its first sentient being takes one middle kalpa, as has already been explained above.
As for the world of sentient beings, this trichiliocosm is formed after being destroyed by fire.
Those whose lives have ended in the Ābhāsvara Heaven are reborn in the abode of Mahābrahmā; born there alone, they become weary and exclaim: "Alas!"
If there were those with a homogeneous lot (*sabhāgatā*) born in this realm, what would be the harm?
Even though such a thought is not produced through the power of mindfulness, when beings from the Ābhāsvara Heaven reach the end of their lives, they are immediately reborn in that place.
The Great Master, in his heart, gave rise to this thought:
"Because I was born through craving,
the world universally calls me the Great Brahmā, the Ancestor of Humanity."
They are born in succession as the Brahmapurohitas, the Brahmakāyikas, and the Paranirmitavaśavartins, down to the Four Great Kings;
and they are born in succession in Uttarakuru, Aparagodānīya, Pūrvavideha, and Jambudvīpa.

At that time, the lifespan of the people of Jambudvīpa was immeasurable years; they delighted in food and drink, were of form born of mind (*manomaya*), possessed bodies that emitted radiance, and moved freely through the air like the devas of the Form Realm.
A kind of earth-essence (*pṛthivī-rasa*) gradually arose, its taste sweet and delicious, its color white like honey, and its fragrance rich and pervasive.

At that time, there was a man whose nature was to crave flavors; upon smelling the fragrance, he conceived a desire for it, took some with his fingers and ate it, and also informed others, who followed his example and took some to eat as well.
Because they consumed solid food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*), their bodily radiance vanished.
Due to the ripening of various karmas, the sun and moon appeared to illuminate the four continents, whereupon the "taste of the earth" (*pṛthivīrasa*) disappeared.

Next, "earth-cakes" (*pṛthivīpiṇḍa*) emerged; their flavor was sweet and delicious, and their color was red like honey. They vied with one another to indulge in eating them, and the earth-cakes likewise vanished.
Next, the forest creepers (*vanya-śāka*) appeared; because they vied with one another in indulging in them, the forest creepers also disappeared.

There grew naturally occurring rice that required no cultivation, which the multitude gathered and ate together. Because this food was coarse, it left behind dregs and impurities, and both the anus and the genitals emerged.
At that time, people would gather fragrant rice to eat according to the timing of their meals.

Later, there was a person whose nature was indolent who took a large quantity of fragrant rice at once to store for his meals; others followed his example, and consequently, the fragrant rice disappeared. They then divided the fields among themselves, fearing its future exhaustion.
Because they developed a sense of stinginess and attachment toward their own plots of land, while harboring intentions to seize those belonging to others, disputes arose.
At that time, the multitude deliberated upon a person of virtue and appointed him as the lord of the fields.
Because he was approved by the multitude, he was called King Mahāsammata (translated here as "Approved by the Multitude").

The king had many sons who succeeded him in succession. The eldest son was named Arcimat; his son was Bhadraśreṣṭha; his son was Viśeṣa; his son was Śānti. These are known as the five kings of the *vivartakalpa* (the aeon of formation).
The son of King Śāntaśālā was named Mūrdhaja; his son was Mṛdvīka; his son was Upamṛdvīka; his son was Sumṛdvīka; his son was Roca; these are known as the five wheel-turning kings (cakravartin).

The son of King Śrīmat was named Śāntika; his son was Viśāntika; his son was Gopani; his son was Goṣṭha; his son was Sudarśana; his son was Mahāsudarśana; his son was Vighuṣṭa; his son was Kanakavarṇa; his son was Saṃbhava; his son was Apagata-mala; his son was Meru; his son was Dhruva-cara; his son was Mahā-ruta-svara; his son was Mahā-ruta-svara-viśiṣṭa; his son was Śamatha-kara; his son was Diśām-pati; his son was Bhadra-rajas; his son was Visāla-kara; his son was Mahādeva. This royal lineage continued through five thousand generations, after which it passed through seven thousand more generations to the king named Asitamṛga.
Finally, there were eight thousand successive generations, the last of whom was King Kaurava; his last son was King Ghatotkaca.
There were nine thousand kings, the last of whom was named Nāgarāja.
There were ten thousand kings; the last of these was Daṇḍakin, who had fifteen thousand sons. The last of them was named Gautama, who was of the Ikṣvāku lineage.
His descendants, the Ikṣvāku royal lineage, numbered one thousand one hundred; the last of these sons was the Ikṣvāku king named Vardhana, also known as King Aśoka-malla.
The king had four sons: the first was named Mukhacandra, the second Hastibhojana, the third Gajapramardin, and the fourth Kinkini; they were known as the Śākyas.
Yan-zhuo had a son named Yan-zhuo-zu; that son’s son was Chi-suo; his son was Niu-ju; and his son was King Shi-zi-jia.
He had four sons: the first was named Jing-fan, the second Bai-fan, the third Hu-fan, and the fourth Gan-lu-fan.
The son of King Śuddhodana is the Bhagavat; his next brother is named Nanda.
King Śuklodana had two sons: the first was named Tiṣya (Devadatta), and the second was named Nandika.
King Droṇodana had two sons: the first was named Aniruddha, and the second was named Bhadrika.
King Amṛtodana had two sons: the first was named Ānanda, and the second was named Devadatta.
The son of the Bhagavat, named Rāhula, marks the end of the Śākya lineage.
Furthermore, kings of other lineages shall arise and establish the teachings according to the Dharma.
Two hundred years after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, there will be a king named Aśoka in a kingdom in Central India.
The Dharma King in Jambudvīpa was the patron during the majority of the [first] councils, causing the Buddha’s teachings to flourish.
Three hundred years later, there was a king in the northwest of Jambudvīpa named Kaniṣka; he served as the patron during the third council, extensively promoting the Buddha’s teachings.

The various Dharma-kings of the lands of Brahmā-India, Kaśmīra, Laṅkā, Kucha (pronounced Qiuci), Nepāla, Zhendan (China), Dali, and Xixia each flourished the Buddha-dharma within their respective countries.

More than a thousand years after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, there was first a king in the land of West Fan (Tibet) named Ya-gri btsan-po. In the twenty-sixth generation, there was a king named Khri sde gtsug brtan btsan, at which time Buddhism first arrived.
In the fifth generation thereafter, there was a king named Zwa-bzang-si-gam-phu, and at that time there was a Paṇḍita named Āditya.
The master of translation was named Dhanesvara; they translated the teachings of the Dharma, constructed monasteries such as Bkra-shis-’od-gsal, and caused the teachings to spread.

Later, in the fifth generation, there was a king named Kri srong lde btsan. This king invited the Great Master Śāntarakṣita, the Guru Padmasambhava, Kamalaśīla, Rba ban Mi tra, and other accomplished practitioners (*siddhas*), together with Vairocana Rakṣita, the venerable Cog ro Klu’i rgyal mtshan, and others—seven individuals in total—to translate the teachings of the Dharma.
The master Kamalaśīla, together with various chief translators, extensively translated the teachings, and the three types of vows flourished and spread throughout the land.

Later, in the third generation, there was a king named Kriṣṇapāśa; his realm was vast. At that time, Jinamitra, Śīlendrabodhi, Prajñāvarman, and others, together with Surendrabodhi, Śīlendra, Śrīghoṣa, Jñānasiddhi, Dharmatāśīla, and so forth, translated and edited those already translated, and translated those not yet translated, causing the teachings to flourish extensively.

The royal lineage of the Western蕃 (Tibet) survives to this day; because there are many translators such as Paṇḍitas, as well as a vast number of masters and spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), the teachings have flourished.
In the northern Mongol kingdom, the previous merit ripened to produce a king named Chinggis (two syllables).
From the beginning, Chinggis was like a Cakravartin King of Iron from the country of Tufan.
His son was named Gan-guo-dai (Genghis), who was then known as Ke-han; he succeeded to the imperial throne and expanded the borders even further.
He had a son named Gu-wei (Kublai), who succeeded to the imperial throne as Emperor Chengzhi.

The second son was named Doro; Doro’s eldest son, named Möngke, also succeeded to the royal throne. The king’s younger brother, named Kublai, succeeded to the imperial throne. He brought various kingdoms under his dominion, and their territories became vast and expansive. He returned to the Buddhist teachings to transform the people through edification, so that Buddhism flourished more brilliantly than ever before.

The Emperor had three sons: the eldest was named Zhēnjīn (True Gold), who was as abundant and complete as the Dharma-treasure of the heavens; the second was named Pángècì; and the third was named Nàmáhè. Each possessed their own innate virtue, and their lineages of succession were likewise established.
This is the beginning from the royal lineage of Śākya down to the present royal lineage.
