translated by Sha-lo-ba, the Great Master of Propagating the Teaching and Tripitaka-holder of the Dharma-nature (Faxing), who was appointed as the General Superintendent of the Buddhist Teachings for the regions of Jianghuai, Fujian, and elsewhere.
Regarding King Sumedha, the first of the royal ancestors: at that time, disputes over land ownership arose, leading to mutual encroachment and theft.
When one first commits theft and is interrogated by the king, yet claims not to have stolen, the first instance of lying arises.
When the king’s law prescribes execution, the unwholesome dharma of killing is then produced.

At that time, sentient beings who committed unwholesome deeds were reborn as animals after their lives ended; next, they were reborn as hungry ghosts; gradually, they were reborn in the hells; and finally, a single sentient being was born in the Avīci Hell.
At the conclusion of the kalpa of formation, sentient beings thus engage in various unwholesome deeds; their lifespans and sense objects diminish.

When the lifespan of the people of Jambudvīpa is eighty thousand years, a single sentient being is born in the Avīci Hell; these two events occur simultaneously, and in this way, the world of sentient beings is formed.
Nineteen intermediate kalpas are spent in the formation of the receptacle world; this constitutes one intermediate kalpa.
Thus, the kalpa of formation consists of twenty intermediate kalpas.
When the lifespan of the people of Jambudvīpa reaches eighty thousand years, the kalpa of abiding begins; this kalpa of abiding likewise lasts for twenty intermediate kalpas.

When they reach the age of ten, the calamity of weapons arises for only seven days and nights; the calamity of pestilence arises for seven months and seven days; and the calamity of famine arises for seven years, seven months, and seven days, during which most perish. Those who remain behold one another and give rise to the thought that such beings are rarely seen; they become harmonious and affectionate toward each other, remaining far removed from killing.
Because wholesome qualities gradually arise, the lifespan and enjoyments further increase and flourish until they reach eighty thousand years.
During the period of increase, a Wheel-Turning King appears and transforms the people according to the Dharma;
during the period of decrease, the Bhagavat appears to rescue and deliver sentient beings.
The Pratyekabuddhas appear in the world during periods of increase and decrease, serving as fields of merit for all sentient beings.
An eon of abiding likewise consists of twenty intermediate eons (*antarakalpa*).

At the beginning of the eon of destruction, the world of sentient beings begins to perish; when no sentient being is born in the Avīci Hell, those whose karma for rebirth there has been exhausted are born in other realms.
If there are those whose karma is not yet exhausted, they will be reborn in the higher hells or in the hells of other worlds.
When the Avīci Hell becomes empty, the higher hells gradually become empty in the same manner, and beings are then born into the realm of hungry ghosts.
In this way, those in the realms of hungry ghosts and animals pass away into space.

Among those in the human realm—excluding the inhabitants of Kuru—they, together with the gods of the desire realm, spontaneously attain the first dhyāna through the natural Dharma and are reborn in the Heaven of the First Dhyāna.

Those born in Uttarakuru are reborn among the gods of the desire realm; those who attain the first dhyāna are reborn in the heaven of the first dhyāna; and those who, without a teacher, spontaneously attain the second dhyāna are reborn in the heaven of the second dhyāna.
From the Avīci Hell up to the Brahma-world, this period likewise lasts for nineteen intermediate kalpas (*antarakalpa*).
Thereafter, seven suns appear over the four continents; at first they do not send down rain, and all medicinal herbs, thickets, and forests wither away.

When two suns appear, the ditches and ponds dry up; when three suns appear, the Gaṅgā River and all others completely parch; when four suns appear, Lake Anavatapta dries up; when five suns appear, the ocean water sinks to the knees; when six suns appear, even the great ocean is exhausted; and when seven suns appear, a single mass of fire rises up from that vessel-world, burning and destroying everything from the Avīci Hell up to the Brahma World for the duration of one intermediate kalpa.
The kalpa of destruction lasts for a total of twenty intermediate kalpas (*antarakalpa*), and the kalpa of emptiness is likewise.

Thus, the kalpas of formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness constitute eighty intermediate kalpas; these eighty together are termed one great kalpa (*mahākalpa*), which serves as the measure of the lifespan for the Brahmakāyika devas and others.
The destruction of the receptacle world occurs in three ways: by fire, water, and wind; the manner of this destruction is as previously described.

After seven such cycles, the world is once again formed, only to be destroyed again by water up to the Second Dhyāna Heaven. From the Ābhāsvara Heaven, great clouds arise and heavy rains pour down; the receptacle world is completely dissolved like salt melting in water, until that water itself dries up.
After one water disaster, there are again seven fire disasters; after passing through seven fire disasters, there occurs once more a single water disaster.
In this manner, when the water disasters have occurred seven times and followed by another seven fire disasters, the world is subsequently formed.
When destroyed by the calamity of wind, it reaches as far as the third dhyāna heaven.
The power of that wind blows apart even Mount Sumeru, let alone anything else.
Although the fourth dhyāna heaven is free from external calamities, when these sentient beings are born there, they are born within palaces; when their lives end, the palaces vanish.

Thus, having fully explained the world of the vessel and its sentient inhabitants, along with their formation and destruction, we turn next to the phenomena of dependent origination through the continuity of cause and effect.
Because they arise by depending upon one another as causes and conditions, they are called "dependently originated."
Dependent origination is twofold: first, external dependent origination; second, internal dependent origination.
External dependent origination refers to the phenomena that constitute the world, such as a seed producing a sprout, as previously explained.
Regarding internal dependent origination: when there is ignorance, there are formations and so forth; this is called "dependent origination in forward order.
When ignorance ceases, formations and so forth cease; this is called "dependent origination in reverse order."

There are seven ways of classifying dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*): furthermore, by way of stages, by way of distant succession, by way of continuous binding, by way of moments, by way of the three time periods, by way of two layers of cause and effect, and by way of the three afflictions.

Regarding the classification by stages (*avasthā*): among the various stages of the afflictions within past lives, the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) are designated as "ignorance" (*avidyā*), because ignorance is predominant therein.
Having stated this, all subsequent explanations are likewise named according to what is predominant.

The formations (*saṃskāra*) and other such factors each possess their own five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*). "Formations" refers to the five aggregates existing during the intervals between the wholesome and unwholesome karmas performed by the practitioner in previous lives.
"Consciousness" (*vijñāna*) refers to the five aggregates present at the single moment of actualizing rebirth within the mother's womb.

Regarding "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*): it refers to the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) during the interval after the consciousness of rebirth (*pratisaṃdhivijñāna*) and before the arising of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).
"Name" (*nāman*) refers to the four aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness;

"form" (*rūpa*) refers to the five stages within the womb—namely, *kalala* (translated as "conjunction" or "coagulated slime"), *arbuda* (translated as "bubble" or "fleshy knot"), *peśī* (translated as "mass of flesh"), *ghana* (translated as "solidification"), and *praśākhā* (translated as "limbs, sinews, and strength")—which constitute name-and-form.

The six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) refer to the five aggregates during the interval from their arising within the mother’s womb through the eyes and so forth up until the meeting of the three, prior to the stage of discerning objects.

Contact (*sparśa*) refers to the five aggregates during the interval when the triad of faculty, object, and consciousness has met, but one is not yet able to discern the causes of suffering and pleasure.

"Feeling" (*vedanā*) refers to the five aggregates during the period from infancy until the stage when sexual desire has not yet arisen, having already understood the distinct characteristics of the causes of the three types of feeling.
"Craving" (*tṛṣṇā*) refers to the five aggregates during the period of one's prime, when one is capable of understanding sexual desire but has not yet engaged in extensive pursuit.
"Grasping" (upādāna) refers to the five aggregates during the stage of seeking everywhere for various excellent requisites.
"Existence" (bhava) refers to the five aggregates during the stage of karma that can draw forth future results, which is accumulated due to such seeking.
"Birth" refers to the five aggregates of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) that link one to the next existence, occurring after death from this life due to the power of karma.
"Old age and death" refer to the five aggregates from the stage of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) up to the stage of sensation (*vedanā*) within the future birth.
The Sarvāstivādins maintain that dependent origination in terms of stages (*avasthika*) is itself "distant continuity" (*prākarṣika*), and that "bondage" (*sāmbandhika*) is likewise so.

The Sautrāntikas do not speak in terms of stages; regarding distant continuity, they hold that ignorance (*avidyā*) is the opposite of knowledge (*vidyā*), and is a mental factor (*caitta*) that serves as the cause for the initiation of activity.
"Formations" refers to the karma that is initiated, namely meritorious, non-meritorious, and immovable karma.
"Consciousness" refers to the arising of consciousness as it is projected by karma.
"Name-and-form" refers to the five aggregates within the womb.
The six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) refer to the arising of the faculties, such as the eye.
Contact (*sparśa*) refers to the conjunction of the three—faculty, object, and consciousness—and is a mental factor (*caitta-dharma*) that performs discernment.
Feeling (*vedanā*) refers to the suffering, pleasure, equanimity, and so forth, produced by that contact.
Craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is the greedy attachment to pleasant objects.
Grasping (*upādāna*) is the seeking after those objects.
Existence (*bhava*) is the karma that brings about future birth, which is initiated by that [grasping].
"Birth" refers to the linking of rebirth through the continuity of karma.
"Old age and death" refers to the final transformation and passing away once that birth has occurred.
The same applies to the continuous bondage.

Regarding the [process occurring] in a single moment (*kṣaṇa*): it means that within one moment, the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) are fully present. Killing through the impulse of greed is [the link of] craving; killing through delusion is ignorance (*avidyā*).

The actual taking of life is volitional formation (*saṃskāra*). The discernment of objects is consciousness (*vijñāna*). The five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) arising simultaneously are collectively termed name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). Abiding in the faculties of name-and-form is called the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*). The conjunction of the three—faculties, objects, and consciousness—is contact (*sparśa*). Feeling (*vedanā*) arises with contact as its cause. Greed itself is craving (*tṛṣṇā*). The various entanglements (*paryavasthāna*) associated with this are grasping (*upādāna*). The two types of karma—bodily and vocal—arising therefrom are becoming (*bhava*). The collective arising of these factors is birth (*jāti*). Their maturation and transformation is aging (*jarā*). Their disintegration is death (*maraṇa*).
Regarding the three time periods: ignorance (*avidyā*) and formations (*saṃskāra*) are subsumed under the past and are termed the causal members (*hetvaṅga*).
Consciousness (*vijñāna*) and the other five members are subsumed under the present and are termed the resultant members (*phalāṅga*).
The three links of craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and existence (*bhava*) belong to the present and are termed the "causal links" of the future.
The two links of birth (*jāti*) and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) belong to the future and are termed the "resultant links."
There are two branches of the past, eight branches of the present, and two branches of the future; thus, there are twelve branches.
Regarding the two layers of cause and effect, there are two: first, the prior limit (pūrvānta), and second, the subsequent limit (aparānta).
Regarding the prior limit (*pūrvānta*): ignorance (*avidyā*) is affliction (*kleśa*) and formative forces (*saṃskāra*) are karma; these two are the causal links.
The five links beginning with consciousness (*vijñāna*), which are produced by those [two], are the resultant links. This constitutes one cycle of cause and effect.
Present craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) are the two factors of affliction (*kleśa*), while becoming (*bhava*) is karma; these three constitute the causes for the future.
That which arises from them—namely birth (*jāti*) and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*)—are the factors of fruition. This constitutes one cycle of cause and effect.
Thus, these twelve links of existence constitute two layers of cause and effect.

With respect to the three delusions, ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and grasping (*upādāna*)—these three are the delusions; while formations (*saṃskāra*) and existence (*bhava*)—these two are karma. These are termed the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*).
The seven links beginning with consciousness are themselves suffering; this is called the Truth of Suffering. This refers to dependent origination in its forward order.
As for dependent origination in its reverse order:
with the cessation of ignorance, formations cease. The cessation of ignorance is the wisdom that realizes the absence of self; this is the Truth of the Path.
If ignorance ceases, the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) that cause birth cease; because the projecting karma ceases, the five links beginning with consciousness cease.
Due to this cessation, the subsequent karma is not initiated, and craving, grasping, and so forth cease.
Because of this cessation, birth, old age, death, and so forth are all likewise extinguished; this is the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*). Having thus explained the Four Truths:

the receptacle world, sentient beings, dependent origination, and the Four Truths are all subsumed within the five categories of phenomena: first, material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*); second, mental phenomena (*citta-dharma*); third, mental concomitants (*caitta-dharma*); fourth, non-associated phenomena (*viprayukta-dharma*); and fifth, unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).

First, regarding material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*), these constitute the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), consisting of eleven factors: the five sense faculties, the five objects, and non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*).
As for the five sense faculties, the atoms (*paramāṇu*) of the eye faculty are like the flowers of the *kustumburu* plant; they reside upon the pupil of the eye, arranged in a horizontal layer.
The atoms of the auditory faculty are like rolled birch bark, residing within the ear canal.
The atoms of the olfactory faculty are like a pair of fingernails, residing within the nasal bridge.
The atoms of the gustatory faculty are shaped like a half-moon, distributed across the tongue.
The atoms of the body-faculty (*kāyendriya-paramāṇu*) are likewise equal in measure to the body itself, pervading the body-faculty from the crown of the head to the feet.
Since the faculty is an object (*viṣaya*), it cannot perceive an external object.
Regarding the five objects: "form" (*rūpa*) refers to the object perceived by the eye, which is of two kinds: first, color-form (*varṇa-rūpa*), and second, shape-form (*saṃsthāna-rūpa*).
Visible color (*varṇa*) consists of four kinds: blue, yellow, red, and white.

Shape (*saṃsthāna*) consists of sixteen kinds: long, short, square, round, high, low, even, uneven, light, shadow, brightness, darkness, cloud, smoke, dust, and mist—these comprise twenty categories in total.
Sound refers to the object-condition of the ear; it is of two kinds: first, those with grasping causes, such as speech; second, those without grasping causes, such as the sound of a drum.

Each of these is further divided into the informative (*vijñapti*) and the non-informative (*avijñapti*), making four types. These are further distinguished by being agreeable or disagreeable, resulting in six varieties.

"Odor" refers to the object perceived by the nose; it is of four kinds: first, pleasant odor; second, unpleasant odor; and because these are further divided into equal and unequal [intensities], they form four distinctions.
Taste refers to the objects perceived by the tongue; there are six kinds: sweet, sour, bitter, pungent, salty, and bland.

Tangibility refers to the objects perceived by the body; it consists of the four great elements as its cause and tangibility as its effect, including smoothness, roughness, heaviness, lightness, cold, heat, hunger, and thirst.
Regarding "unmanifest form" (*avijñaptirūpa*), it refers to the form that consists of restraint (*saṃvara*), non-restraint (*asaṃvara*), and that which is neither;
this constitutes the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).
Second, as for "mental factors" (*caitasika*), there are six, namely: eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mental consciousness; these six constitute the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*).
Third, as for the mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*), there are forty-six.
First, the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*) are of ten kinds: feeling (*vedanā*) refers to experiencing;
perception (*saṃjñā*) refers to causing the mind to apprehend an object.
Volition (*cetanā*) means causing the mind to move;
attention (*manasikāra*) means causing the mind to take an object as its focal point;
resolve (*adhimokṣa*) means causing the mind to confirm an object, which is to say, it means causing the mind to be free from timidity regarding the focal object.
Desire refers to longing;
contact refers to the harmonious engagement with an object;
wisdom refers to discernment.
Mindfulness (smṛti) means causing the mind to clearly remember its object without forgetting;
concentration (samādhi) means causing the mind to focus single-pointedly on a single object.
These ten types, which pervade all states of mind, are called the universal mental factors (mahābhūmikadharma).
2. There are ten great wholesome mental factors (*mahābhūmika-kuśala-dharma*). "Faith" (*śraddhā*) means that which causes the mind to be clear and pure toward its object.
"Heedfulness" (*apramāda*) means the constant practice of wholesome dharmas and the guarding of the nature of the mind.
"Pliancy" (*praśrabdhi*) means the adaptability of the mind.
Equanimity (*upekṣā*) means causing the mind to abide in impartiality;
self-respect (*hrī*) means abiding with reverence toward all virtues and those who possess virtue;
and shame (*apatrāpya*) means perceiving dread in regard to transgressions.
Non-attachment means not being attached to the outflows (*āsrava*);
non-hatred means not delighting in harming sentient beings;
non-harming means having compassion for sentient beings so as to prevent them from suffering injury or affliction.
Vigor (*vīrya*) refers to the mind’s courageous intensity regarding what is wholesome.
These ten types, which pervade all wholesome minds, are called the Great Wholesome Ground Dharmas (*kuśalamahābhūmika*).

Third, the Great Affliction Ground Dharmas (*kleśamahābhūmika*) consist of six kinds. Delusion (*moha*) refers to ignorance, which is precisely non-illumination, lack of knowledge, and lack of clarity; it is *avidyā*.
Heedlessness (*pramāda*) refers to the failure to cultivate various wholesome qualities due to negligence;
indolence (*kausīdya*) refers to a lack of vigor and fortitude in the mind;
and lack of faith (*āśraddhya*) refers to a lack of clarity and purity in the mind.
Lethargy (*styāna*) refers to the mind-body continuum’s lack of serviceability (*akarmanyatā*), which carries the sense of being dull and heavy;
restlessness (*auddhatya*) refers to the mind’s lack of tranquility.
These six types of universal afflictions of the mind are called the *mahābhūmika-kleśa-dharmas* (great ground-dharmas of affliction).

Fourth, regarding the great unwholesome mental factors (*akuśala-mahābhūmika*), there are two types: first, lack of shame (*āhrīkya*), which means causing the mind to lack reverence toward all virtues and those who possess virtue;
second, lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*), which means failing to perceive fear regarding various transgressions.
These two types, which pervade all unwholesome minds, are called the universal unwholesome mental factors (*akuśala-mahābhūmika-dharma*).
Fifth, the minor defilement mental factors (*parīttakleśabhūmika-dharma*) consist of ten kinds: *krodha* (anger) refers to causing the mind to flare up with resentment;
*upanāha* (enmity) refers to repeatedly dwelling upon the object of anger, harboring a grudge, and refusing to let it go.
Flattery (*śāṭhya*) refers to crookedness of mind;
deception (*māyā*) refers to delusive transformation;
envy (*īrṣyā*) refers to an inability to tolerate the virtues of others.
*Pradāśa* (malice) refers to the stubborn adherence to one's own faults, by which one does not accept reasoned admonition;
*mrakṣa* (concealment) refers to hiding one's own faults;
*mātsarya* (avarice) refers to causing the mind to be stingy regarding one's own teachings and wealth.
*Stambha* (conceit) refers to the mind becoming arrogant and self-indulgent due to attachment to one's own physical form, strength, lineage, and so forth.
*Vihiṃsā* (harmfulness) refers to inflicting oppression upon others.

These ten types are abandoned solely through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), pervade the level of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna-bhūmi*), and are termed the "mental factors of the minor affliction ground" (*parīttakleśabhūmika-dharma*).

Sixth, regarding the indeterminate factors (*aniyata-dharma*), there are eight types: *vitarka* (applied thought) is defined as the characteristic of causing the mind to move coarsely toward an object;
*vicāra* (sustained thought) is defined as the characteristic of causing the mind to move subtly toward an object;
*kaukṛtya* (remorse) refers to the regret over actions that have been poorly performed.
Sleep (*middha*) refers to that which is unable to sustain the continuity of body and mind, causing the mind to become dull and withdrawn;
hatred (*vyāpāda*) refers to that which causes the mind to take pleasure in harming sentient beings and the like;
craving (*lobha*) refers to attachment to the outflows (*sāsrava*).
Pride (māna) is that which causes the mind to be haughty and self-important;
doubt (vicikitsā) is that which causes the mind to be hesitant.
Because these eight types [of mental factors] lack fixed presence in the preceding stages, they are termed "unfixed" (aniyata).
The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* and the *Pañcaskandhaprakaraṇa* explain eleven types of wholesome states: among these, the internal realization of the Four Noble Truths is termed non-delusion (*amoha*).

Within the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), the grasping of the impure as pure, as well as defiled attention (*manasikāra*) and resolve (*adhimokṣa*), are termed improper attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*) and false resolve (*mithyādhimokṣa*).

Among the root afflictions (*mūlakleśa*), that which is a portion of defiled wisdom (*kliṣṭā prajñā*) consisting of inverted deliberation regarding the principles of the truths is called incorrect awareness (*asamprajanya*).

Among the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), that which is a portion of defiled mindfulness (*kliṣṭā smṛti*) being unable to clearly retain its objects is termed loss of mindfulness (*muṣitasmṛtitā*).
That which causes the mind to wander among various objects of focus and defiles the factors of meditative concentration is called distraction (*vikṣepa*).
The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* does not state this.
Among the aforementioned mental factors (*caitta*), with the exception of sensation (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*), all are subsumed under the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).
This concludes the section on mental factors.

Regarding the non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*), there are fourteen types; among them, "acquisition" (*prāpti*) is a distinct entity that exists in association with the continuity of sentient beings and with moral discipline (*saṃvara*).
That which is incompatible with those vows is a distinct entity called "non-acquisition" (*aprāpti*).
The commonality of activities performed by various classes of sentient beings is called "homogeneity" (*nikāyasabhāga*).

When one is born among the non-conceptualizing beings (*asaṃjñisattva*) in the heavens, there exists a dharma capable of causing the cessation of mind and mental factors; this is a real entity called the "fruit of non-conceptualization" (*asaṃjñiphala*).
Furthermore, there is another distinct dharma capable of causing the cessation of the mind and mental factors, which is called the "attainment of non-conception" (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*).

It is named the "attainment of non-conception" because it is a meditative state characterized by the absence of conception; alternatively, it is called the "attainment of non-conception" because within this attainment, conception is absent.
As it is said below, the cessation of perception, feeling, and so forth within the continuum of a noble one (ārya) is a real entity (dravyasat), termed the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti).
From the time a sentient being is first born until they have not yet died, this interval is called the life-faculty (jīvitendriya).

That which was previously non-existent and now exists is called "arising"; that which causes it to abide for a moment is called "abiding"; transformation is called "aging"; and deterioration is called "impermanence"—these are the four characteristics of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*).

That which expresses its own substance is called the "name-body" (nāmakāya); that which expresses the ultimate meaning is called the "phrase-body" (padakāya); and that which serves as the clothing for these two is called the "syllable-body" (vyañjanakāya).
These constitute the fourteen dharmas.
Furthermore, in terms of meaning, the internal refutation of the harmonious assembly is termed "disharmony.
The results of karma performed ripen upon oneself; just as a debt is never lost, so too do objects and the like constitute factors dissociated from consciousness.
In the Sarvāstivāda school, matter (rūpa), mind (citta), and mental factors (caitasika) are distinct entities.
The Sautrāntika masters maintain that these three dharmas are merely provisional designations for specific states.
Excluding feeling (vedanā) and perception (saṃjñā), the forty-six mental factors and the dissociated formations (viprayukta-saṃskāra) are termed the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha).
Regarding unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), they shall be understood below.
Thus, these material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) are called the ten elements (*dhātu*); excluding non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*), they consist of the ten [elements] beginning with the eye.
The mental phenomena (*citta-dharma*) comprise seven elements, namely the six consciousnesses and the mind-faculty element (*manas-indriya-dhātu*).
When categorized by their bases (*āyatana*), these seven factors are subsumed within the single base of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).

Mental concomitants (*caitasika-dharma*), dissociated phenomena (*viprayukta-dharma*), unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), and non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*) are collectively termed the *dharmadhātu* and are also called the *dharmāyatana*.
Thus have been explained the five dharmas of the knowable, the five aggregates (*skandha*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the eighteen elements (*dhātu*).

Chapter Three: The Chapter on the Dharmas of the Path (*Mārgadharma-varga*). Furthermore, as for the "Path": it refers to those who possess few desires and are content, who are endowed with the spiritual lineage (*gotra*), and who, having physically and mentally withdrawn from various forms of worldly distraction, abide in the precepts of a lay follower (*upāsaka*) and so forth; such persons should diligently listen to the Dharma.

Having heard extensively, one should contemplate the meaning of what has been heard; having contemplated it, one should practice cultivation, which means one should cultivate *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.

Those with excessive greed should cultivate the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*); those with excessive anger should cultivate the contemplation of loving-kindness and compassion (*maitrī-karuṇā-bhāvanā*); those with excessive delusion should cultivate the contemplation of the analysis of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-vibhaṅga-bhāvanā*); those with excessive self-clinging should cultivate the contemplation of the analysis of the elements (*dhātu-vibhaṅga-bhāvanā*); and those with excessive distraction should cultivate the contemplation of counting the breath (*ānāpāna-smṛti-bhāvanā*).

Once śamatha and vipaśyanā have been accomplished, by cultivating resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), one understands the internal and external body in accordance with the Dharma; this is called the application of mindfulness to the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*).
Understanding suffering, pleasure, equanimity, and so forth in accordance with the Dharma is called the application of mindfulness to feelings (*vedanāsmṛtyupasthāna*).
To understand the six consciousnesses and mental factors according to the Dharma is called the application of mindfulness to the mind (*cittasmṛtyupasthāna*).
To understand perception, formations, and the unconditioned according to the Dharma is called the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*).
Cultivating these four dharmas constitutes the provision of wisdom (*jñānasaṃbhāra*).
Having accumulated the provisions for the Path, one cultivates the path of application (*prayoga-mārga*).

Within the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*), one abandons evil that has already arisen, prevents evil not yet arisen from arising, increases good that has already arisen, and brings about the arising of good not yet arisen; these four dharmas are called the four right efforts (*samyak-pradhāna*), which the text refers to as the right abandonments (*samyak-prahāṇa*).

Within the stage of the summit (*mūrdhan*), there are the concentration of wholesome desire, the concentration of wholesome diligence, the concentration of wholesome mental attention, and the concentration of wholesome discernment; these are called the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*).

Within the stage of patience (*kṣānti*), practicing mundane right view is called faith (*śraddhā*); delighting in the cultivation of wholesome dharmas is called diligence (*vīrya*); clear mindfulness without forgetting is called mindfulness (*smṛti*); focusing one-pointedly on a single object is called concentration (*samādhi*); and knowing what to adopt and what to abandon is called wisdom (*prajñā*). Because the cultivation of these five dharmas can give rise to wholesome qualities, they are called the five faculties (*pañcendriya*).

Within the stage of the Supreme Mundane Dharma (laukikāgradharma), one cultivates the five—faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom—which are able to destroy their opposites; therefore, they are called the five powers (pañcabala).
This constitutes the path of preparation (prayogamārga).
Within the stage of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), the thorough knowledge of the Four Truths is called Right View (*samyagdṛṣṭi*).

The arousal of right speech is called Right Thought (*samyaksaṃkalpa*); speaking correctly according to the Dharma is called Right Speech (*samyagvāk*); abandoning unwholesome karma is called Right Action (*samyakkarmānta*); relinquishing wrong livelihood is called Right Livelihood (*samyagājīva*); aspiring toward wholesome dharmas is called Right Effort (*samyagvyāyāma*); clear mindfulness without forgetting is called Right Mindfulness (*samyaksmṛti*); and one-pointed concentration on a single object is called Right Concentration (*samyaksamādhi*).
These eight factors are called the eight branches of the noble path.
This is the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).

The conceptual afflictions (*vikalpakleśa*) and their acquisitions (*prāpti*) etc., which are abandoned by the path of seeing—namely, with respect to the truth of suffering in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*)—are: greed, hatred, pride, ignorance, doubt, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), the view of attachment to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), the view of grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), and false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
The two truths of origination (*samudaya*) and cessation (*nirodha*) each eliminate three views;

thus, there are fourteen (seven times two). Those to be abandoned by the truth of the path (*mārga-satya*) exclude the aforementioned two views, totaling thirty-two across the four truths of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
In the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), for each of the four truths, hatred is excluded, totaling twenty-eight; it is the same for the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Thus, there are eighty-eight [defilements] to be abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) across the three realms.

Within the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*): clearly recollecting wholesome phenomena is called the awakening factor of mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*); discerning what to adopt and what to reject is called the awakening factor of wisdom (*prajñā-saṃbodhyaṅga*); aspiring for and seeking diligent effort is called the awakening factor of energy (*vīrya-saṃbodhyaṅga*); realizing untainted joy (*anāsrava-prīti*) is called the awakening factor of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*); the body and mind functioning according to their nature is called the awakening factor of pliancy (*praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*); not being led astray by worldly phenomena, being without attachment or hindrance, is called the awakening factor of equanimity (*upekṣā-saṃbodhyaṅga*); causing the mind to abide in its object is called the awakening factor of concentration (*samādhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
Cultivating these seven branches is called the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

Through this path of cultivation, one abandons the innate afflictions (*sahaja-kleśa*), the acquisition of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-prāpti*), and the neutral (*avyākṛta*) as well as the tainted wholesome (*sāsrava-kuśala*) states.
Within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there are four—greed (*rāga*), hatred (*dveṣa*), delusion (*moha*), and ignorance (*avidyā*)—each possessing nine grades, totaling thirty-six.
Within the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), in the first dhyāna, anger is excluded; the remaining three [defilements] each have nine grades, totaling twenty-seven.
The same applies to the second, third, and fourth dhyānas.
The realm of form (rūpadhātu) consists of one hundred and eight factors in total; the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) is likewise.
Thus, the factors to be abandoned through the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga-prahātavya) across the three realms total one hundred and fifty-two.

Next, regarding the realization of the ten dharmas of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), they are: right view, right thought, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration, right liberation, and right knowledge and vision of liberation.

This is the path of no-more-learning (aśaikṣamārga). Chapter Four: The Category of Fruition-Dharmas (Phaladharma-varga). Furthermore, regarding "fruition": as previously stated, one takes the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (bodhipākṣikadharmas) as the means to resolve the mind toward liberation from saṃsāra. For those of sharp faculties, the maximum duration for realizing arhatship is three lifetimes: in the first lifetime, one cultivates the wholesome roots conducive to liberation (mokṣabhāgīya), which is called the path of equipment (sambhāramārga); in the second lifetime, one cultivates the wholesome roots conducive to penetration (nirvedhabhāgīya), which is called the path of preparation (prayogamārga); and in the third lifetime, one realizes the fourth fruit of the śramaṇa, just as described above.

Because those of dull faculties and the indolent are not fixed [in their progress], they are like those who are "candidates for the fruit" (pratipannaka), such as the candidate for the first fruit of stream-entry (srotāpatti-phala). The four are called fruits.

The candidate for stream-entry, prior to the path of preparation (prayoga-mārga), perceives that the nature of both the sentient beings and the physical environment (bhājana-loka) is suffering; this is the Truth of Suffering (duḥkha-satya). Furthermore, the causes thereof—namely karma and afflictions (kleśa)—are called the Truth of Origination (samudaya-satya). That which brings about liberation from these is the Truth of Cessation (nirodha-satya). Furthermore, the cause for that [cessation] is the Truth of the Path (mārga-satya).

When one has mastered the cultivation and, through that sequence, realizes the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), one first contemplates the four characteristics of the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*): it is called "impermanent" because its nature is subject to transformation; it is called "suffering" because it consists of the three types of suffering; it is called "empty" because the substantially existent [self] is not identical with the aggregates; and it is called "non-self" because the substantially existent [self] is distinct from the aggregates. Thus, one directly realizes these four cognitions (*jñāna*).

Next, regarding the observation of the four natures of the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*): because it is the principle of the seed of suffering, it is the cause (*hetu*); because it is the principle of the manifestation of suffering, it is origination (*samudaya*); because it is the principle of the continuity of suffering, it is birth (*jāti*); and because it is the principle that conforms to suffering, it is condition (*pratyaya*). One thus realizes these through the four wisdoms of direct realization.

Next, regarding the four characteristics of the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*): because the cause of suffering has ceased, it is cessation; because the fruit of suffering has subsided, it is tranquility; because it transcends the outflows (*āsrava*), it is sublime; and because it is liberated from saṃsāra, it is detachment. These are the four wisdoms realized through direct perception.

Next, regarding the fourfold nature of the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*): it is called the "Path" (*mārga*) because it has the sense of being a universal vehicle; it is called "Suchness" (*nyāma*) because it accords with correct principle; and it is called "Practice" (*pratipad*) because one cultivates non-conceptual wisdom (*amanasikāra-jñāna*), thereby realizing the three types of knowledge through direct manifestation.
These fifteen are called those who are candidates for the first fruit.
As for the sixteenth, because they have eternally transcended all states of existence through that Truth of the Path, they emerge and directly realize a single gnosis.
These sixteen constitute abiding in the first fruit (*srotāpatti-phala*).

Having realized the sixteen aspects (*ākāra*) of the Four Truths and brought their cultivation to maturity, one who has abandoned the first five of the nine grades of afflictions (*kleśa*) to be severed through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) of the desire realm is a candidate for the once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin-pratipannaka*);
having abandoned the sixth grade, one is a once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin-phala*).
That "once-returner" (sakṛdāgāmin) returns once more to the desire realm (kāmadhātu) to undergo one further birth.
Because the three lower grades [of defilements] within the desire realm have been abandoned through a single birth,

and because the aspects of practice have been realized and cultivated to maturity such that seven or eight grades [of defilements] are abandoned, this is called the "candidate for non-returning" (anāgāmipratipannaka).
The abandonment of the ninth grade is called the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*).
As for that non-returner, having completely exhausted all afflictions of the desire realm, they will certainly not return to be born in the desire realm again.

Having attained mastery in the cultivation of the modes of practice for the various stages of the higher realms through direct realization, one abandons the nine grades of afflictions within each of the four dhyānas and the four formless attainments.

Beginning with the abandonment of the first grade of the first dhyāna and ending with the abandonment of the eighth grade of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), one is termed a "candidate for arhatship" (*arhattva-pratipannaka*).
Upon abandoning the ninth grade, one is termed the "fruit of arhatship" (*arhattva-phala*).
As for that Arhat, because he has severed all afflictions of the three realms without remainder, he is named an Arhat.
A sutra states:
"Regarding the eight stages such as the Stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā-bhūmi*), the Śrāvaka’s path of accumulation (*sambhāra-mārga*) is the Stage of Dry Wisdom."
When sensual craving is withered and dried up, and the sense organs do not encounter their objects, this cultivated virtue is called the Stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuklavidarśanā-bhūmi*).

As for the Stage of the Lineage (*gotra-bhūmi*), it refers to the Path of Application (*prayoga-mārga*); one will certainly not become a Buddha, but is fixed in the lineage of a Śrāvaka or a Pratyekabuddha, and is thus named the Stage of the Lineage.

The stage of the eight persons (*aṣṭamaka-bhūmi*) refers to the period from the candidate for the first fruit up to the fruit of arhatship; it is called the stage of the eight persons because there are eight individuals therein.

The stage of one possessed of vision (*darśana-bhūmi*) refers to one who abides in the first fruit; it is called the stage of one possessed of vision because they have directly realized and perceived the aspects of the four noble truths.
The "Thin Ground" (tanubhūmi) refers to the fruit of once-returning (sakṛdāgāmiphala); because the afflictions of the desire realm have been largely severed, it is called the Thin Ground.

The "Ground of Freedom from Desire" (vītarāgabhūmi) refers to the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala); because one has abandoned the craving and other defilements within the desire realm, it is called the Ground of Freedom from Desire.

The stage of "having completed what was to be done" refers to the Arhat; having known suffering, abandoned its origin, realized its cessation, and cultivated the path, it is called the stage of having completed what was to be done.
The stage of the śrāvaka consists of the three [stages] of the non-returner (anāgāmin), the once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin), and the arhat; these are called the stage of the śrāvaka.

Regarding the stage of the pratyekabuddha: as previously described, one practices the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma) solely with the desire for oneself alone to realize bodhi. Having thus resolved to practice for a hundred great eons, one is born in one's final body during a world-age devoid of a Buddha, and without relying on the instruction of a teacher, achieves the realization of a solitary enlightened one (pratyekabuddha).
There are two types: first, the rhinoceros-like; second, those who travel in groups.
The rhinoceros-like metaphor refers to one who dwells alone and possesses the conduct of an noble being.
Those of the group-traveling class dwell together with a multitude.

The one who has attained ultimate perfect enlightenment is he who, for the sake of bringing all sentient beings to buddhahood, gives rise to the supreme bodhicitta of great compassion regarding the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment as previously described; who serves all Buddhas to bring them complete joy; and who practices the six perfections for the benefit of others, thereby attaining ultimate buddhahood after three incalculable eons.

In the past, Śākyamuni Tathāgata was a potter named Mahāprabha, who first conceived the aspiration for enlightenment in the presence of the Tathāgata Mahāśākya. From then until the beginning of the first asaṃkhyeya kalpa, he served seventy-five thousand buddhas, the last of whom was named Ratnaśikhin.
During the second asaṃkhyeya kalpa, he served seventy-six thousand buddhas, the last of whom was named Dīpaṃkara.
During the third asaṃkhyeya kalpa, he served seventy-seven thousand buddhas, the last of whom was named Abhibhū.
Regarding those six perfections: with a heart of great compassion, he bestowed all manner of requisites upon sentient beings.

When he was the Prince Viśvantara, his perfection of giving reached ultimate fulfillment; even when his limbs were severed while he had not yet abandoned desire, his mind harbored not the slightest resentment.
When he was the Rishi Kṣāntivādin, his two practices of patience and ethical discipline were brought to ultimate perfection.
When he was the son of a Brahmin, seeing the Buddha Tiṣya dwelling in the fire-element samādhi, he forgot to lift one foot for seven days and nights; circumambulating him, he praised him, saying:

"Within this world of heaven and earth, Or in the abodes of the gods throughout the ten directions, There is no place equal to the palace of the Sugata, Nor any like the chamber of the All-Knowing One."
"The Great Śramaṇa, a bull among men, has searched the earth, mountains, and forests, yet none can equal him.
Having praised him thus, he immediately transcended nine kalpas and brought the perfections (pāramitās) to ultimate fulfillment.

Abiding at the site of perfection upon the Vajrāsana, during the first watch of the night he subdued the hosts of Māras; during the final watch of the night, through the diamond-like samādhi (*vajropama-samādhi*), his two practices of concentration and wisdom reached ultimate fulfillment.
Thus, prior to subduing the Māras while seated upon the Vajrāsana, he had fulfilled the accumulations of merit and wisdom through three incalculable eons and served all the Buddhas.

Although the six perfections were complete, he remained in the body of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*) until, sitting upon the Vajrāsana, he realized the path of seeing and the path of cultivation, attaining perfect enlightenment.

Within the Śrāvaka vehicle, at the time of the cause, it does not explain the thorough understanding of the selflessness and emptiness of all phenomena, the practice of compassion, the threefold emptiness of the wheels [of agent, action, and object], or the characteristics of the ten stages; at the time of the fruit, it does not explain the reward body (*saṃbhogakāya*) or the four wisdoms (*caturjñāna*), and so forth.
The Dharma of Perfect Enlightenment is comprised of six aspects: namely, body, wisdom, abandonment, benefiting others, great compassion, and the perfection of qualities.
Regarding the body, there are two types: first, the form-body (*rūpakāya*), and second, the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
The form body (rūpakāya), endowed with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, is the self-nature body (svabhāvakāya).
Because it delivers the gandharvas and the piṅgalas, it manifests as the king of the gandharvas and as a wheel-turning sage king (cakravartin); this is the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya).
Nevertheless, the Buddhas and others differ in various respects, such as their lineage (*gotra*), physical stature, lifespan, buddha-fields, and the faculties (*indriya*) of their disciples.
As for the two aspects of the *dharmakāya*, they are identical among all Buddhas in possessing the ten qualities of one beyond training (*aśaikṣadharma*).
The wise possess two kinds of knowledge: first, universal knowledge (*parijñā*), and second, correct knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*).

Universal knowledge refers to the thorough comprehension of the essential nature of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense bases (*āyatana*) along with their causes and effects; therefore, it is called universal knowledge.

Regarding "right knowledge" (samyag-jñāna): it refers to knowing the dharmas such as impermanence within the Four Noble Truths; hence it is called right knowledge. Regarding "abandonment" (prahāṇa), there are two types:
first, the abandonment of the afflictive obstructions (kleśāvaraṇa); second, the abandonment of the cognitive obstructions (jñeyāvaraṇa).

The abandonment of the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*) refers to the counteracting of the root afflictions such as greed, as well as the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), so as to bring them to cessation.
Second, the abandonment of the cognitive hindrances (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) refers to the counteracting of the factors that obscure the nature of objects and time, so as to bring them to cessation.
There are two types of benefiting others: first, establishing sentient beings in liberation by abandoning what is contrary [to it] and causing them to abide in the Path;
second, establishing sentient beings in the happy realms by abandoning the evil [realms] and causing them to abide in the wholesome.
Great compassion and its virtues will be explained below.

Regarding what the noble ones call "virtues," there are eleven types: namely, the absence of conflict (*araṇā*), the knowledge resulting from prayer (*praṇidhijñāna*), the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), the six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), the four meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*), the ten spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*), the eight bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), and the three types of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

Regarding "the absence of contention" (*araṇā*): it refers to relying on the mind of the fourth dhyāna to cultivate meditative concentration (*samādhi*) with the thought, "May all sentient beings not give rise to afflictions by taking me as an object. It is thus called the absence of contention.

Aspiration-knowledge (praṇidhijñāna) refers to that which arises by relying on the mind of the fourth dhyāna; preceded by aspiration, it induces a knowledge that accords with reality, and because one understands in accordance with one's aspiration, it is called aspiration-knowledge.
The four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) are: first, the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*), because of knowing the names of all phenomena;
second, the analytical knowledge of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*), because of correctly knowing the meaning;
third, the analytical knowledge of expression (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*), because of correctly knowing words and phrases.
The four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) are so named because they consist of the correct knowledge of principles.
As for the six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*):
first is the power of the miraculous realm (*ṛddhividhi-abhijñā*), which consists of traveling through stone walls and other obstacles without impediment.
The supernormal power of the divine ear (*divya-śrotra-abhijñā*) is so called because it thoroughly cognizes all various sounds, whether near or far.
Third is the supernormal power of the divine eye (*divya-cakṣur-abhijñā*), which is able to apprehend, as appropriate, forms in all directions—whether obstructed, extremely subtle, or distant.
Fourth is the supernormal power of knowing the minds of others (*paracitta-abhijñā*), because it can know whether the minds of others possess desire or not.
Fifth is the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-abhijñā*), because it knows the events of one's own and others' past existences.
Sixth is the supernormal power of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya-abhijñā*), because it knows all mundane and supramundane paths.
The first five [superknowledges] are with outflows (*sāsrava*) and rely upon the fourth dhyāna;
the sixth is without outflows (*anāsrava*) because it relies upon the ninth [dhyāna].
Regarding the four dhyānas: the first dhyāna possesses five factors (*aṅga*): first, vitarka; second, vicāra; third, prīti; fourth, sukha; and fifth, samādhi.
In the second dhyāna, there are four factors: first, internal serenity; second, joy; third, bliss; and fourth, meditative concentration (samādhi).
In the third dhyāna, there are five factors: first, equanimity; second, right mindfulness; third, right discernment; fourth, the experience of bliss; and fifth, meditative concentration.

Within the fourth dhyāna there are four factors: first, the purity of equanimity; second, the purity of mindfulness; third, neither-painful-nor-pleasant sensation; and fourth, meditative concentration (samādhi).

Regarding the four formless attainments: when practicing the preparatory application, one contemplates infinite space, infinite consciousness, and nothingness; thus, at the time of entering meditative absorption, one eliminates the basis of form and [abides in] the remaining four aggregates.

As for the fourth name: because perception (*saṃjñā*) is dull and inferior—meaning that ignorance (*avidyā*) predominates—it receives the name "Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception" (*asaṃjñi-nāsaṃjñin*);
because there is a dull and inferior perception, it is called "Non-Non-Perception."

In this successive order, the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception are called the four formless realms.
If the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) is added, these are also called the nine successive attainments (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*).
As for the four immeasurables (*catvāry apramāṇāni*), they are loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*).
Among these four, the first two have non-hatred (*avyāpāda*) as their essential nature; sympathetic joy is the feeling of joy (*saumanasyavedanā*), and equanimity is non-attachment (*alobha*).

Regarding the objects of focus: they serve as antidotes, respectively, to the malice and harm found among sentient beings in the desire realm, as well as to the joy and gratification, sensual desire, and hatred.

As for the eight liberations: based on the first and second dhyānas, the first is the liberation in which one possesses internal perception of form while observing external forms; through the transformation of the perception of impurity into the perception of a bluish corpse, one observes form by means of form.

Second, the liberation consisting of perceiving external forms while having no perception of internal form; following the three bases of the internal perception of formlessness, one dwells having fully realized through bodily experience the pure liberations of the dhyānas, perceiving all forms as pure and radiant.
These three types [of formless attainments], together with the four formless absorptions (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), constitute the next four liberations (*vimokṣa*).
The attainment of the cessation of sensation and perception (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha-samāpatti*) is the eighth liberation.

Based on the mind of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), noble beings (*ārya*) loathe coarse sensation and perception; by means of a tranquil absorption, they cease the mind and its mental factors (*citta-caitta*), which is termed the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).

The ten totalities (*kṛtsnāyatana*) refer to the pervasive observation of earth, water, fire, wind, blue, yellow, red, white, as well as space and consciousness—the two boundless bases (*anantya-āyatana*).
Based on the fourth dhyāna, one takes visible forms of the desire realm as objects and pervasively observes these bases, such as earth, without any gaps or interruptions.
Among these ten, the first eight have non-attachment as their essence; the latter two are, respectively, emptiness and consciousness, taking the formless realm as their intrinsic nature.

As for the eight bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*): first, perceiving internal forms while observing external forms that are few; second, perceiving internal forms while observing external forms that are many; third, perceiving no internal forms while observing external forms that are few; fourth, perceiving no internal forms while observing external forms that are many.
With no perception of internal form, one contemplates external forms as blue, yellow, red, and white; these constitute four [liberations]. Together with the preceding four, they form eight.
Among these eight, the first two are like the first liberation, the next two are like the second liberation, and the final four are like the third liberation.
If that is so, what distinguishes the eight spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) from the three liberations (*vimokṣa*)?
Answer:

In the prior cultivation of the liberations, one is only able to turn away [from the object]; in this cultivation of the spheres of mastery, one is able to master the object of focus so that it ultimately does not arise again, regardless of one's desire.

The cultivation of liberation and so forth serves two purposes: first, to ensure that the various afflictions already severed are further distanced; second, to attain superior mastery over meditative concentration.

This enables the arousal of qualities such as the absence of conflict (*araṇā*) and the sublime supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), through which one can transform all things and act as the cause for various functions, such as prolonging or relinquishing life.
The three samādhis are emptiness (śūnyatā), signlessness (animitta), and wishlessness (apraṇihita).
Emptiness samādhi refers to meditative concentration (samādhi) associated with the two modes of activity (ākāra): emptiness and non-self.
The signless samādhi refers to the meditative concentration associated with the four aspects of the truth of cessation.
Because nirvāṇa is signless—being free from the ten signs—it is called "signless."
Because it can take that [emptiness] as its object, it receives the name "signless" (*animitta*).
As for the concentration of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-samādhi*), it refers to meditative equipoise associated with the ten modes of activity (*ākāra*) directed toward the remaining truths.
Because the impermanent and the causes of suffering are objects to be reviled;
because the Path is like a raft and must necessarily be abandoned;

Because these qualities are shared by Arhats liberated through both parts, Pratyekabuddhas, and Tathāgatas, they are called "shared qualities.
Those liberated through wisdom lack the three types of meditative concentration and the four immeasurables.
The unique qualities of a Tathāgata consist of eighteen kinds, namely: the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the three foundations of mindfulness, and one great compassion.

The ten powers (*daśabala*) are: first, the power of knowing what is possible and what is impossible; second, the power of knowing the maturation of all karmas; third, the power of knowing the meditative absorptions, liberations, concentrations, and attainments; fourth, the power of knowing the superior and inferior faculties of beings; fifth, the power of knowing the various inclinations of beings; sixth, the power of knowing the various elements (*dhātu*); seventh, the power of knowing the paths leading everywhere; eighth, the power of recollecting past abodes; ninth, the power of knowing death and rebirth; and tenth, the power of knowing the exhaustion of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).

The four fearlessnesses are: first, fearlessness regarding perfect enlightenment; second, fearlessness regarding the destruction of the outflows; third, fearlessness regarding the proclamation of obstacles; and fourth, fearlessness regarding the proclamation of the path.
Because one possesses the power of wisdom and thus has no fear of others, it is called "fearlessness" (*vaiśāradya*).

Regarding the "three foundations of mindfulness" (*trīṇi smṛtyupasthānāni*): when the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma and his disciples are entirely respectful and able to correctly receive and practice it, the Tathāgata does not give rise to joy on account of this; rather, he dwells in equanimity with right mindfulness and right situational awareness (*samprajanya*). This is called the first foundation of mindfulness of the Tathāgata.

If the assembly of disciples fails to show respect and does not correctly receive and practice [the teachings], the Tathāgata, conditioned by this, does not give rise to sorrow or distress; rather, he relinquishes it and dwells in right mindfulness and right clear comprehension. This is called the Tathāgata’s second station of mindfulness.

Among the assembly of disciples, some are respectful and able to correctly receive and practice [the teaching], while others are disrespectful and do not correctly receive and practice it. The Tathāgata, regarding this, gives rise to neither joy nor sorrow; he remains equanimous, dwelling in right mindfulness and right clear comprehension. This is called the Tathāgata’s third application of mindfulness.
These three all take mindfulness and wisdom as their essence; therefore, they are called "foundations of mindfulness" (*smṛtyupasthāna*).

As for "great compassion" (*mahākaruṇā*), it refers to observing the world throughout the six periods of day and night to discern who is suffering and who is happy, and who should be disciplined, thereby providing benefit and happiness according to their needs; hence, it is called great compassion.

The eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*) of the Tathāgata, the three ways in which he need not guard himself (*trīṇy arakṣāṇi*), and so forth, as taught in the Mahāyāna, have never been heard of in the Śrāvaka vehicle.

Chapter Five: On Unconditioned Phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*). Furthermore, unconditioned phenomena are of three kinds: first, space (*ākāśa*); second, cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*); and third, cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

Regarding what is called "unconditioned space" (*ākāśa-asamskṛta*): space exists as a mere presence, having non-obstruction as its essential nature; because it is unobstructed and pervades all places, it is termed "unconditioned space," within which matter (*rūpa*) moves.

All other doors, windows, apertures, gaps, as well as all spaces characterized by light or darkness, and the *āgāsa-rūpa* (space-like matter), are not unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Second, regarding the unconditioned of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha-asaṃskṛta*):

this refers to the truth revealed by the two paths of vision (*darśana-mārga*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), wherein outflow-free wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) eliminates all obstructive defilements; this is termed the unconditioned of analytical cessation.

Regarding the third unconditioned phenomenon, non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*): it refers to that which can eternally obstruct the arising of future dharmas. Its attainment is distinct from the former [analytical cessation] and is thus called non-analytical cessation.
Its attainment does not depend on analytical discernment but occurs solely due to the deficiency of conditions; hence it is named non-analytical cessation.

These three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) are accepted by the Sarvāstivādins as having substantial reality (*dravyasat*), whereas the Sautrāntikas maintain that they lack any constructed nature (*kṛtaka*).
Question:
Is not *tathatā* (suchness) itself unconditioned?
Answer:
That is precisely *anātman* (selflessness), because the Śrāvaka vehicle does not teach the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*).

Regarding the selflessness of persons (*pudgalanairātmya*), it consists of the sixteen aspects such as impermanence and so forth. The aspects of the three truths are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), while the aspect of the truth of cessation (*nirodhasatya*) is exclusively the dharma of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*), and not any other dharma.
Thus, these five objects of knowledge—the environment, sentient beings, the path, the fruit, and the unconditioned—comprehensively encompass all phenomena that can be known.

The phenomena of the environment and sentient beings are the Truth of Suffering; the causes that bring them about are the Truth of Origination; the two phenomena of the path and its fruit are the Truth of the Path; and the unconditioned phenomenon of analytical cessation is the Truth of Cessation.

The two types of unconditioned phenomena—space and non-analytical cessation—and the three types of unconditioned phenomena [in total] are not subsumed under the Four Noble Truths; for the two truths of suffering and its origin consist of contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*), while the two truths of the path and cessation consist of uncontaminated phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*).
Thus have been explained the objects of knowledge— both mundane and supramundane, conditioned and unconditioned.

This *Treatise on Elucidating the Objects of Knowledge* was composed by the late Emperor Yuzong, whose sagely brilliance observed all things and whose divine wisdom discerned with clarity. Out of compassion for those deluded by false views and grief over the obstructions blocking the true path, he requested the Imperial Preceptor, the Dharma King, to bring benefit and happiness to sentient beings; thus, it expounds the ultimate truth of supreme enlightenment—the great principles regarding the sequence of practice from its beginning to its end.

Vast yet subtle, profound yet classical, like ancient brocade and refined gold, these teachings are utilized according to the capacity of the vessel; their meanings are subsumed into five categories, yet they ultimately converge into one.

What is called the "sentient and insentient world" is not like the divergent grasps of the blind men feeling the elephant—some claiming it is a single vital breath (*ekaprāṇa*), others saying it is spontaneous nature (*svabhāva*). It points directly to the mind’s creation, providing a detailed clarification of the beginning of the kalpa, encompassing that which lies beyond the eight directions and analyzing that which exists within the smallest atom (*paramāṇu*); it is like an image reflected in a mirror, or a finger held in the palm.
Regarding the Dharma of the Path, its causes consist of fewness of desires and contentment, the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation, and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment.
Regarding the Dharma of the Fruit, its results consist of the provisions, the stage of application, the path of seeing, the path of cultivation, and the path of no-more-learning.
That which is called "unconditioned" (asaṃskṛta) refers to the principle of the Truth of Cessation (nirodha-satya) among the Four Noble Truths.
Because these five categories comprehensively encompass all phenomena that can be known, it is said to "reveal the treatise on the knowable."
